speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROBABLE DATE OF PRESENTATION
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Finance whether he is in a position to indicate when the budget will be presented?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROBABLE DATE OF PRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize that I have indicated on two or three occasions that the budget would be presented at an early date. I am doing the best I can with the situation, but I must say that it will be two weeks from now at the earliest before I shall be able to present the budget. There has been a very considerable increase in the number of matters that make demands upon my time, and while a large amount of work is being done on it I do not think we can get it to the stage, of completion until the time I have indicated. While I am on the subject I might refer to the fact that there are many rumours in the press and elsewhere as to what the budget will contain. I want to say that all those rumours without exception are entirely unfounded.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROBABLE DATE OF PRESENTATION
speechtext: Does the minister read them all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROBABLE DATE OF PRESENTATION
speechtext: I have not read them all. In the nature of the case they must of necessity be unfounded. I do not know what the budget will contain; the government does not know wdiat the budget will contain. I will not know' until almost the last moment before the budget is presented.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROBABLE DATE OF PRESENTATION
speechtext: The press is in just about as good a position as you are to prophesy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROBABLE DATE OF PRESENTATION
speechtext: I am not prophesying. I think it does far more harm than good to make statements, some of which are rather plausible on their face, as to what the budget will contain. I want to make it very emphatic that nobody knows what will be in the budget or has any ground whatever for making predictions as to what the contents of the budget will be.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROBABLE DATE OF PRESENTATION
speechtext: Perhaps it is the way the press have of making suggestions to the government, and the minister mistakes them for predictions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROBABLE DATE OF PRESENTATION
speechtext:
Perhaps so.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL IN CIVILIAN CAPACITY-FLORENCE COLLIERIES, SYDNEY, N.S.
speechtext: I should like to direct two short questions to the Minister of Labour based on telegrams which I received yesterday. One was from the steel workers' lodge 1064 at Sydney protesting against the employment of seventy-six members of the Joliette regiment as labourers in the steel plant while local labour was available. The second concerns the failure of the operators to accept the decision of the adjustment board in Nova Scotia and reinstate three employees at the Florence collieries. Is the minister in position to say whether his department can intervene in these disputes?-because they might mean a serious interruption of production.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL IN CIVILIAN CAPACITY-FLORENCE COLLIERIES, SYDNEY, N.S.
speechtext:
I got my hon. friend's question just before I came into the house. The Department of Labour had no knowledge of this situation at Sydney until a telegram was

Labour Conditions
received from the steel workers, I think on June 1. We checked the situation. It is true that seventy-six members of the Joliette regiment stationed at Sydney volunteered their services while on learn during the weekend and were employed at local wage rates, subject, I am informed, to the usual deductions for income tax. As to the question of employing members of the armed forces in a civilian capacity while civilians aTe seeking employment, my information is that there are no civilians in the Sydney area who are seeking employment of the kind undertaken by the men from this regiment.	_
The second question dealt with the dismissal of three employees at the old Sydney collieries in Nova Scotia. Word was received yesterday by my department that the adjustment board set up under the agreement between the United Mine Workers of America and the Dominion Steel and Iron Corporation had adjudicated on the dismissal of three employees, and while the arbitration board finds that both the company and the men were at fault, it recommended that the men should be reinstated. My department immediately got in touch with our resident officer at Fredericton, who in turn informed the company that their refusal to reinstate these men was a breach of section 17 of P.C. 1003. That is how, the matter stands at the moment. The general manager of the company was absent at the time and the message was conveyed to the general superintendent, who I am informed got in touch with the general manager with reference to the opinion on the matter held by the Department of Labour. I hope to be able to give to my hon. friend some word over the week-end as to the conclusion of the dispute.

I must state to the

Canadian wool board, administration, $500,000.

Has any change been made from last year? Manitoba and British Columbia did not participate in the bonus because under the agreement that was made the provincial governments had to put up fifty per cent. I think it is very unfair. I do not need to speak for British Columbia because-

War Appropriation-Finance
Mr, ABBOTT: If my hon. friend will allow me, the payment of the subsidy, which is a producer's subsidy, is under the Department of Agriculture and has nothing to do with the operations of the Canadian wool board. I think my hon. friend's inquiry should be directed to the Minister of Agriculture.

The price of wool in Canada was set by the wartime prices and trade board at 25 cents to the producer, while in the United States the O.P.A. set the price at 45 cents. The wool is all handled and controlled by the united nations wool pool. Why, then, is not the price in Canada as high as it is in the United States?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In the first place, so far as I am aware, there is no united nations wool pool. The United States price has been higher than our price, which is the case with a good many other commodities. Incidentally the price in Canada is somewhat higher than 25 cents a pound as mentioned by my hon. friend. I have the 1944 prices here. The lowest price is 28 cents, and from that the prices range, depending on grade and quality to 33 cents and higher per pound.
Were subsidies not paid in the past on wool coming in from South America?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Certainly not during the past year, and I am advised that at no other time has a subsidy been paid.
A subsidy was granted in the early days of the war on wool coming in from South America, and I wondered if any had come in. I know that their wool is of a very poor quality, dirty and tangled.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We permitted the import, but there was no subsidy paid because I am advised that none came in.
It did not come in evidently because of its quality.

While it is true, as the parliamentary assistant has said, that the subsidy on wool is paid under the Department of Agriculture, is it not a fact that the price of wool in this country is based on the price in the London market of Australian wool plus the freight from Great Britain to Canada? That was one of the reasons for the subsidy, to help make up the difference. At least that is the information we have from the wool growers association.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised that the price of wool is fixed at the laid-down cost of New Zealand and Australian wool in this country,
From London?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No, from New Zealand and
Australia, whichever country it happens to come from.
How long is this subsidy policy to continue? Is it to continue after the war?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am afraid I am not in a position to say how long it will continue. If I venture into the field of prophecy, I think it is likely that we shall have to avail ourselves of subsidies until at least the end of the war, as part of the. price control policy.
Would the minister put on the record the amount of wool which has been imported in the last three years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have not that information here, but I can get -it and give it to my lion , friend, if that would be satisfactory.
Is there a subsidy on shoddy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The corporation sustained a loss of S5.95 last year on shoddy.
They do trade in it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.

Wool is being stored in large quantities in buildings throughout the country. Does the matter of storage come within the scope of this department, or is it handled elsewhere; and if so, could the minister give particulars of the contracts for storage?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The company has its inventory stored in about forty warehouses. It pays the usual storage charges for warehousing its product, as any other merchant would do. I have a list here of the warehouses which are used; to be exact, there are thirty-nine. I do not know whether my hon. friend wants me to give him the list. It is a long one.

I would like the hon. member to place the list on the record; also to indicate if all contracts for storage are on a uniform basis, if persons are employed by the government to secure storage buildings, and how the entire system of storage is handled for the department.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I find that the list I have here is last year's list. There is one more name to add to it, and I have not that name here. I suppose one should be prepared for
War Appropriation-Finanse

all these questions, but I had not thought that we would require to table the list. However, I can get it. I do not know whether it need be printed in Hansard; that is as the committee wishes. If my hon. friend or any other hon. member is particularly interested I can see that a copy of the complete list is furnished. Perhaps that course would be preferable to printing the list in Hansard. Would that be satisfactory to the hon. member for Wellington South?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As to the basis on which these warehousing charges are paid, I am advised by the comptroller of the board, who is in front of me, that the contracts are on the usual basis. We would have to get particulars of each individual deal. There is no objection to doing that; I should be quite ready to furnish that information; but again I am afraid I have not got it here. There would be a certain amount of work in getting it, but if either the committee or any individual hon. member wants it of course I shall be glad to get it.
Is the storage based on so much per pound or per hundred, or does it vary with different buildings?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised that some of it is on a poundage basis, and some of it is on an annual rental basis, where it is expected that the whole of the space which can be rented can be used. It varies from warehouse to warehouse, depending on the circumstances.
Where the contract is made on an annual basis, is the contract with the government, or the owner of the building, or in some other way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The contract is between Canadian Wool Board Limited, the corporation whose estimates we are now discussing, and the warehouse company, or the owner of the warehouse, as the case may be. .

This board has been set up for a matter of two years. It was created under order in council P.C. 1853 of March 10, 1942. Unfortunately we have not the latest financial statement to Inform us as to the operations of the company during the last year. In the previous year the company had a net loss of approximately $34,000. I would like a little enlightenment on the matter of the commissions on sales, totalling $11,345.82.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is that in last year's figures or this year's figures?

Those are last year's figures.
IMr. Abbott.]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have just received the statement of this year.
What were the operating profits or losses for the year ended March 31, 1944?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The net operating loss for the year ended March 31, 1944 was $221,296.11. I think my hon. friend has the comparative figure for last year.

Yes. I have these
figures: $36,246 last year, as against $221,296 this year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is correct.
Could the minister break that down into, let us say, commissions on sales, warehouse expenses, administrative expenses, office furniture and equipment

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes. Commissions on sales, $58,857.40, and a small item of $665.90 for discount on sale; total $59,523.30. Under warehousing expenses are included storage and handling, insurance, inter-warehouse freight, miscellaneous repairs, bales and bags, sampling and testing. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have here a three or four page document setting out the regulations issued by the Canadian wool board respecting rates of commission to registered wool warehouses on Canadian fleece wool in 1944. It gives the information which I take it my hon. friend wishes to have, but since I am not an expert on wool, I should be glad if he would indicate more definitely exactly what he wants.

I am not especially
interested in any one particular item. This is an amount which is paid to the regular firms

War Appropriation-Finanse
operating in wool. Is that the object of the commission? This corporation carries on business through regular wool dealers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Regular wool brokers, wool dealers; that is correct.
What is the rate of commission paid?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The sole purchaser of Canadian-produced wool is the corporation, and it buys only graded wool through the registered warehouses. Agents, collectors or the wool growers' association may be licensed by the board to operate on behalf of the registered warehouses, but payments are made directly to the grower by the registered warehouse on the basis of grades and prices set by the board, and the warehouse is allowed the uniform commission. The wool sold by the board for civilian requirements is sold at prices in conformity with the domestic ceiling, and on all importations of wool yarns, fibres et cetera, the board assumes the position of any private importer as regards import subsidies and applies to the stabilization corporation for subsidies required to avoid a loss on its own account.
What is the rate of commission paid these wool firms?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The table I have referred to will give an idea of the rates:
For services rendered, a registered warehouse shall be entitled to commissions on the following basis:
Section 1-2J cents per pound on all range wool and western domestic wool in the fine and i blood grades.
Section 2-3J cents per pound on all other grades of range wool and on all other grades of western domestic wool.
Section 3-3J cents per pound on all grades of eastern wool-Ontario, Quebec and the mari times.
These rates per pound on the net weight of the respective classifications are the full rates which will be paid by the board for all services rendered; payments to licensed agents; handling, grading, normal weight loss, insurance and all carrying charges until the wool is taken over by the board; loading graded wool on railway car or truck, and any other expenses incidental to the .proper operation of a registered warehouse.
There is a good deal more information with regard to commissions of other types.

Can the parliamentary assistant tell us whether we are getting sufficient wool now? Two years ago we were 8,000,000 pounds shy, and that meant that the farmers would have to clip another million sheep to make up the shortage. At that time, two years ago, when the people were making blankets, they used seventy per cent shoddy and a year ago fifty per cent. Can the parliamentary

assistant make a statement on the progress that has been made in the provision of wool?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The situation is fairly satisfactory. As of March 31, 1944, the holdings of wool by the board, including stocks owned jointly with the United Kingdom, were 27,500,000 pounds, clean basis. With the war picture now changed and no longer demanding the holding of such large stocks as were necessary until recently for civilian and military purposes, the policy is to liquidate a substantial part of the present inventory.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have no wish to delay the passing of this item and I am sure the parliamentary assistant is anxious to avoid any possible delay, but I do want to call his attention to a part of the debate that took place last night after the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) had asked some questions with reference to the potato subsidy which had been claimed and had been paid to the producer. On page 3441 of Hansard, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton said:
Coming back to the -potato subsidy, we all know what was claimed to have been paid the producer. Since the investigation we know what was actually paid. Would the parliamentary assistant tell us what was actually paid the producers? The investigation showed the amount that was paid.
Then he went on to say:
But he had to pay a certain price to the producer. It is claimed that he paid $3.50 for the first part of August and $3 for the latter part. What did he actually -pay?
The parliamentary assistant then said he was afraid he did not have the information here. Then the member for Victoria-Carleton said that perhaps Mr. Van Buskirk might know. Some time before the debate ends-
And that is why I am rising now.
-I would -ask the parliamentary assistant to give the information to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, because if it is not readily available now it should be available before the debate ends. This is a vital part of the whole situation, as I see it.
The parliamentary assistant was good enough to say:
I shall see what information I can get.
I rise now not to open the matter again but to ask for the information that was promised.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I had in mind dealing with all these points together when we had completed the various estimates, but I might
346S
War Appropriation-Finance

as well deal now with the point raised by the member for Victoria-Carleton and the leader of the opposition. I made inquiries this morning as to the prices paid the producers in the case referred to, and I am advised that the board's investigator did disclose what prices were paid. They were found to be prices below the ceiling; otherwise a subsidy would have been properly payable. I am sure, however, it would be improper to disclose the private business of a private firm, in this house or elsewhere, as to prices paid for a particular commodity, and particularly so since the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton is a competitor, I believe, of the shipper in question. Mr. Chairman, I think
the time has come when the house should regain what it used to have, namely, some control over war expenditures, as they appear in these estimates. We have just seen voted the sum of $140,000,000, and we have been divested of any control whatsoever in connection with that expenditure.
We now come to the office of the auditor general, one which at one time in Canada was most honoured. I have criticized this report at length since the war began. Shortly after confederation a great auditor general

arose-the late Mr. McDougall-and he operated under the treasury of Mr. Mackenzie, who used to sleep on the strong-box. Well, there is no one in Ottawa now to sleep on the strong-box. Alexander Mackenize was a Liberal and an economist. Where is he today? The statue of him is away in the back yard-and that is a fitting place for him at the present time, the way money is being spent. In those days the auditor general's office was an important one. A civil war was fought in England to enable parliament to get control over all expenditures. Since this war began we have lost all control over war or civil expenditures, and all economy or retrenchment is forgotten.
What control has this parliament over any expenditures? Here we have an expenditure of around four billions of dollars. Last year I read to hon. members a letter received from the auditor general's office-I refer of course to the present auditor general, Mr. Sellar, a very good official, so far as I know. At the time I received the letter he was secretary to a minister of finance. In his letter he stated that he had no control over anything contained in war appropriation bills. The procedure has been amended somewhat so that now there is a comptroller of the treasury who has certain duplicate duties under the Minister of Finance. I sympathize with the minister, because I realize he carries a very heavy burden. He is the pivot of the whole public service, and bears a heavy share of work. However, I fail to see the usefulness of this particular division.
As hon. members know, there is now sitting a war expenditures committee. Where they are, I do not know. They have been lost, strayed or stolen. We have not had one report from them, and we have now reached the seventieth day of the session. I have yet to see one report from the war expenditures committee.
What are the functions of the auditor general and comptroller? Those functions are set out. They do not state that he is an official of the Minister of Finance. Rather he is an official of parliament and is responsible to parliament for every dollar spent. But we might as well go home, and stay home, for all the control this parliament has over war expenditure. All the boards have been appointed, and about 46,000 orders in council have been passed. Do hon. members think that orders in council do not involve the expenditure of money?
The auditor general makes his report a few days after the opening of parliament, and in it we find the public accounts. It is a very good report. If he sees anything wrong it is his duty to report it to the house, but up to

War Appropriation-Finance
last session very little reporting had been done. I do not see the hon. member for Temiscouata in his seat, but 1 know he would give the other house more work. I suggest the report of the auditor general might very well be referred to another branch of parliament in another place, where some of these expenditures could be considered.
I notice the Minister of Fublic Works is smiling. It was said that they could not get paint, but I notice they have enough money for yellow paint-"Site No. 1", "Site No. 2", "Site No. 3"-disfiguring not only the pavement but also the landscape on which we want to spend millions of dollars to beautify the city. Let us get rid of some of the extravagance right around parliament hill.
The auditor general has lost control over war expenditures and civil expenditures. He has not the functions he used to have. These are all with the comptroller now. A report may be presented to the comptroller of the treasury for payment and as long as it is within the four corners of the appropriation bill it is paid. Some of those reports cover almost a quire of paper. The information is given on the back of the paper, but there is very little check on the expenditure. No great banking system could maintain itself if it had not a better auditing system, nor could a department store or a railway company. The war expenditures committee never report to parliament till near the end of the session. They conduct their business as a star chamber. 1 doubt if the auditor general could get into that committee. I say the time has come for us to put on the brakes in respect of some of these war expenditures. I have the report of the auditor general before me and I think it is a good report for the money that has been spent. The vote is only $290,000. I am criticizing the system, not the officials.
I believe the time has come when parliament should try to regain some of the control over war and civil expenditures which has been lost. The auditor general reports to the house on anything that he considers to be wrong, and the report is a rather heavy volume. Our war expenditures amount to over four billion dollars and, as I say, the House of Commons should try to regain some of the lost control over expenditures.

Old age pensions and pensions to the blind. $6,942,250.

This vote of $6,942,250 is a war vote described as being for old age pensions and pensions for the blind; in the course of my remarks I propose to deal with the old age pension, although most of these remarks will also apply in the case of the blind pension. The war vote is for approximately $7,000,000, and in addition there is a vote in the ordinary estimates for 831,569,780, of which $43,280 is for departmental administration, and the remainder, 831,526,500, is for old age pension and the blind pension. I take it that the reason why we have a war vote this year for the first time under this head is order in council P.C. 6367, passed on August 10, 1943, entitled "order in council authorizing making of agreements with provinces governing old age pensions." That order in council, as the minister explained on July 24 of last year, provides for the possibility of an increase of $5 a month in the case of a single pension, namely, an increase from $20 to $25, of which of course the dominion would pay three-quarters and the province would pay the remaining quarter. The first paragraph of the order in council reads as follows, and, I think, is very significant:
Whereas the Minister of Finance reports-
1.	That under wartime conditions-
And I emphasize those words.
-It has become desirable and necessary to provide additional assistance to old age pensioners and blind pensioners.
As recently as May 29 the minister announced further changes. He described them in the house on that day, and his explanation will be found at page 3304 of Hansard. There are several changes; for example, in the case of a single pensioner the allowable income from sources other than the old age pension is now restored to 8125 a year, it having been cut to $65 by the order in council passed last August.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was cut only by leaving the statutory rule where it was.

War Appropriation-Finance

But the effect was that the single old age pensioner could earn or receive only $65 over and above his old age pension. There are certain other changes which are beneficial, but they do not go very far. One of them has to do with restrictions on residence in the case of an applicant for old age pension who has spent part of his life out of the dominion. As I understand it, the change is that now, if, for example, an applicant has been out of Canada for five years of the last twenty, he can get a pension by waiting a year, the original provision of course being that an applicant must have been in Canada for 5.844 days out of the twenty years preceding his application for pension. So that there is some easing there, although it does not cover the need. I have a case where a woman now eighty-seven years of age was born in Canada and has lived here seventy-eight years of her life, but it so happens that she was out of Canada eight years in the last twenty. Under the law as it stood before these changes were made, she would have had to wait sixteen years from the day she returned to Canada. Now she will have to wait four years. In other words, she will be ninety-one before she can qualify for pension. I think that when the change was made it would have been better to provide that if a person had lived in Canada for twenty years of his life, or since he became forty or even thirty-five years of age, he would be qualified. That, I think, would have been much fairer.
There are several other changes-one with regard to an applicant moving from one province to another; another with regard to applicants who have been out of the country' on ships or fishing; also a provision with regard to collecting from the estate upon the death of a pensioner. I think those changes are beneficial. But the minister in explaining them went a little further than just saying what they were. He also made a statement on policy, which will be found on page 3305 cf Hansard, in these words:
These changes represent the result of a very careful examination of the steps which the dominion would recommend to make the present legislation meet the immediate practical problems without radical revision of the whole scheme.
He went on to discuss contributory old age pensions, which I submit constitute an entirely different problem from the problem of noncontributory pensions which we have at the present time. He said that a scheme of contributory pensions could be introduced only after there had been discussions between the dominion and the provinces. I think he was right in that statement. But it is obvious that there will be no provision for contribu-
[Mr. Ilsley.l
tory old age pensions during the present session. It is also obvious that there will be considerable delay before a scheme of contributory old age pensions can be instituted, and that even though it were, it would not help the present recipients of old age pensions or those Canadians of, say, over sixty years of age at the present time. Probably they would have no time left in which to contribute to the scheme, and no funds with which to contribute; they, I think, must be covered by a non-contributory scheme; I do not see that they are going to be helped very much by a contributory scheme. So that I suggest to the minister and to the committee that there are two separate problems, contributory pensions and non-contributory pensions, and that our particular job at the present time is to deal with the latter.
I think there are two serious defects in the government policy with regard to noncontributory old age pensions. The first is that the government, as announced by the minister the other day, is against any radical revision of the present scheme. The government is making wartime changes only. I read from the order in council of last August in which the minister set out that it was to meet the wartime conditions, and that is true of the changes which have been made this week, again by order in council rather than by amendment to the old age pension legislation; they are all based on a wartime need, the wartime position.
Then what changes are made are made only after there has -been much pressure from members and even from a committee of the house; last year w'e had a report from the special committee on social security; it appears in Votes and Proceedings of July 23, 1943. Hon. members will find in paragraph 5 of the report of that committee the following recommendation:
That the government review the existing regulations governing old age pensions, pensions for the blind, and war veterans' allowance, and consider the advisability of adjusting the eligibility age to a lower level and of increasing the amount of pension.
Pressure has also been brought to bear by the press and the people in many parts of Canada, as well as by most of the provincial governments. So that the second defect in the present government policy is that the government is declining to take the lead in settling this old age pension problem.
I am convinced that the government is wrong in each case, and very seriously wrong. After all that our Canadian people have gone through in the war, and with the Atlantic charter as drawn up by those two great leaders,

War Appropriation-Finance
Mr. Churchill and President Roosevelt, emphasizing freedom from fear and freedom from want for all the peoples of the world, I think we have developed in Canada a new standard of values. We are placing far greater value on men and women and far less value on money and material things than we did before the war. We are emphasizing the human angle in our whole course of life. There is a new spirit abroad in this country as there is in all the other countries of the united nations, and I suggest that this parliament should recognize that fact and act accordingly. And right here, in the old age pension scheme, is a good place to make a start. It is a good place for us to put into action this new and better spirit that is abroad in the land. I am convinced that there is a very widespread and firmly held opinion in Canada that these older Canadians, these senior citizens, are not being cared for adequately, that they are being treated harshly. Quite a few of them come into my office when I am at home in Vancouver, during the short time the house is not sitting, and when they find that they are not eligible, because of some particular regulation or restriction in the act, they feel that they are being treated cruelly, and I must say that in many cases I get the same impression myself. The restrictions are much too severe.
I believe that the policy is not right. I propose to mention several features of the old age pension situation in Canada to-day which I think should be remedied. First of all the amount of the payment. As I said in the opening of my remarks, that amount is $20 under the act, and an additional $5 provided by order in council of last fall, making a total of $25 in the case of a single person. Then some of the provinces are paying an additional amount by way of cost-of-living bonus; at least that is so in British Columbia; they describe it as a cost-of-living bonus. I believe Alberta and British Columbia are each paying an additional $5, making a total of $30 for single persons. Other provinces pay smaller amounts, but there are great difficulties in this arrangement. For example, in British Columbia it is paid only to those who get a pension there or where there is an agreement with another province; an Albertan moving into British Columbia can get a cost-of-living bonus because of the agreement between the two provinces; and it is payable only so long as the pensioner continues to reside in British Columbia. I suggest that the payment of this additional $5 should be on a national basis; it should be dominion-wide. The single old age pensioner should get at least $1 a day,
which means a little over $30 a month. That should be the very minimum in all parts of Canada.
Then the allowable income over and above the old age pension is now a maximum of $125 a year. Provision should be made that a pensioner could with his earnings bring the total income up to at least $50 a month. Anything he earned over and above the pension would be earned by his own efforts, and he should be encouraged to make as much as possible in the way of earnings.
Again, pensioners should be allowed their home without any value in the way of income being placed upon it. There is a very arbitrary way of setting income value on real property. I have here the regulations under the act, and as the minister knows, regulation 17 (a) (2) reads:
For the purpose of determining the income of any applicant the pension authority shall take into account all sources of income including

And then comes (2):
-real property at the rate of not less than 5 per centum of the assessed value or market value thereof (whichever be considered the more equitable standard) exclusive of encumbrances-
And mind you, there may be absolutely no income from this real property.
-or, in the discretion of the pension authority, the net income from real property if the net income exceeds five per centum of the assessed value or market value thereof (whichever be considered the more equitable standard) exclusive of encumbrances.
I suggest that actual income alone should be counted in deciding whether or not the pensioner is getting the allowable income.
Then the age for qualification should be reduced. The minister said in his statement on May 29 that several of the provinces had asked that it be reduced, and he went on to say that if all or substantially all asked he would give consideration to making provision for the reduction. I suggest that the dominion should take the lead and not wait for the provinces. There was a report tabled last year known as the Marsh report on social security for Canada. Members are, or they ought to be, familiar with that report. Doctor Marsh deals with old age pensions, and I quote from page 73 with reference to the age of eligibility:
Review of the forty or more systems of old age assistance, contributory and non-contributory, effective in the world to-day clearly shows that the generally accepted view as to the proper age when consideration should be given to retirement from work and provision of security is 65 for men and 60 for women.
That is the finding of the government's own appointee.
War Appropriation-Finanse

Further the act and the regulations should be humanized. I have already given some instances of where that could be done. These are the days of social security. The Canadian people want real social security. May I give an example of that. This year the British Columbia legislature passed unanimously a resolution dealing with old age pensions, which reads as follows:
Whereas this house notes with satisfaction that the government of the Dominion of Canada has seen fit to increase allowances made under the Old Age Pensions Act:
And whereas these increases have been made under the War Measures Act, thereby limiting these increases to the period of the duration of the war;
And whereas the allowances are still less than this house considers adequate:
And whereas the government of the Dominion of Canada did not increase the amount of income the pension applicant may have before becoming ineligible for pension:
And whereas the government of the Dominion of Canada did not decrease the age at which persons shall become eligible for pension:
Therefore be it resolved, that this house petition the government of the Dominion of Canada urging that the Old Age Pensions Act [DOT]be amended to provide that the maximum pension be raised to $365 per annum and that the maximum income be raised to $500 per annum and that the age at which persons become eligible for pension be reduced to sixty-five years for men and sixty years for women.
And be it further resolved, that this house petition the government of the Dominion of Canada, urging that the Old Age Pensions Act and its regulations be so amended that property used by pensioner as his home and contributions reasonably expected from children, donations, and benevolences be not treated as income.
I think that resolution of the British Columbia legislature is typical of the feeling of the people in most parts of Canada. They are not the only ones who think the regulations should be humanized. I would again refer hon. members to Doctor Marsh's report at page 70. He points out that in Great Britain a far larger, percentage of the people over seventy years of age are able to qualify for government assistance than in Canada. Four-fifths of all the people over seventy in Great Britain are able to qualify, whereas in Canada he says it is unlikely that more than fifty to sixty-five per cent of the people over seventy are able to qualify for assistance of any kind, including old age pensions or relief or any other kind of assistance. He goes on to say:
While it would be tempting to assume that this is an indication of the greater comfort of the aged in Canada, and their greater ability to provide for themselves with savings or through their families, independent of the state, such an assumption is hardly sufficient to reconcile the entire difference. When one turns to examination

These are very significant words in a young country like Canada which prides herself on being up-and-coming and wealthy.
-of the old age pensions administration in Canadian provinces, one finds a major portion of the answer to this discrepancy between British figures and our own; an answer which is a good deal more realistic and less to the credit of the Canadian people as a whole. Examination, for example, would reveal written into the act itself, and especially into the regulations-but most of all practised in the administration-a rigid system of eligibility requirements set on a very low level, which makes it difficult for many aged, persons, genuinely in need of some form of assistance on a permanent continuing basis, to qualify for allowances. These provisions include:
1.	Citizenship;
2.	Residence restrictions, both dominion and provincial;
3.	Means testing in terms of the applicant's personal income, personal property qualifications, and even the assumption of income from property where in fact such income does not exist.
I referred to that in dealing with real property. The report continues:
4.	The principle, zealously adhered to in certain provinces, of the responsibility of the children, to the point of assuming that income is actually forthcoming from children -for the support of the applicant, even in cases where it is not;
5.	Scaling-down of allowances below the amount permitted by the statute, cn the grounds that the pensioner does not require even that amount of pension which is found to be the arithmetical maximum payable after the exhaustion of all statutory, regulatory and administrative means-test procedures.
Therefore I say that the act and the regulations should be humanized. I then come to the question of citizenship. We listened in the house a few Weeks ago to statements of several hon. members to the effect that certain old people who came here from other lands had never been naturalized, so that they now find themselves unable to qualify for pension. They also find .themselves unable to become naturalized because they cannot speak either English or French. That is a situation which should be remedied. I do not believe that the remedy should be by changing the naturalization provisions, but I suggest to the minister that consideration be given to using the test of domicile as defined in our Immigration Act for deciding whether or not a person is entitled to old age pension. I believe that should be decided on their Canadian citizenship under the same provisions or similar provisions to those found in the Immigration Act. The definition is found in section 2, paragraph (e) of the Immigration Act, and is as follows:
(e) "domicile" means the place in which a person has his home, or in which he resides, or to which he returns as his place o-f permanent

War Appropriation-Finance
abode, and does not mean the place where he resides for a mere special or temporary purpose;
(i) Canadian domicile can only be acquired, for the purposes of this act, by a person having his domicile for at least five years in Canada after having been landed therein within the meaning of this act.
If a person has become domiciled in Canada under provisions such as those contained in the Immigration Act then the twenty years could run from that time or they could be used as a basis rather than the present basis which, I believe, is British citizenship. The individual must be a British subject.
There are other respects in which the act and the regulations could be improved; I have pointed out just a few. But I repeat that a radical revision of the whole scheme is needed now, not after the war. At that time the suggestion will be made that we postpone it until we settle post-war problems. This is something that should be done now without delay. The dominion must take the lead in bringing about a revision of the scheme and changes should be on a statutory basis and not by order in council under the War Measures Act.
I suggest that old age pensions should be administered not by the Department of Finance-with all due respect to the minister and his own department; I think it is not their job to deal with old age pensions-but. by the new department of social welfare. About all the responsibility the dominion government takes at the present time-and this is taken, of course, through the Department of Finance-is to pay three-quarters of the cost and to check the accounts. Doctor Marsh deals with that situation in his report. He objected strenuously to the act and the regulations being administered in the provinces by the workmen's compensation boards, and by the way, I understand that at the present time only one or two of the provinces are so administering old age pensions; most provinces have set up a separate old age pension authority.
In his report Doctor Marsh used these words at page 71:
The tendency in workmen's compensation administration is to assess eligibility on relatively hard and fast lines and then to apply the eligibility schedule strictly. Scaled to different earnings levels and to a variety of accident cases, this is less apt to produce harsh results. Scaled to what is supposed to be a minimum and to a need which is relatively equal for all eases, it can only produce inequities. Unfortunately, federal supervision reinforces these tendencies, through the fact that the old age pensions authority on the federal level is located in the Department of Finance. The supervision of provincial administrations consists almost exclusively of audit and financial
control, the result being a restrictive influence on provincial administrations which is easily-reflected in a repressive attitude towards the applicant.
The speech from the throne pointed out that we were to have a department of social welfare, the work of which was described as follows:
A department of social welfare to organize and to assist in administering activities of the federal government in the fields of health and social insurance.
Then, in the resolution on the order paper at the present time with regard to the setting up of this department of social welfare we find that one of its duties is set out in this way:
. . . to assume the management and control of and to consolidate in such department matters relating to the social security and welfare of the people of Canada.
So that I suggest to the committee that old age pensions should come under this new department of social welfare. In that department should be experts trained in social welfare problems, the idea being that in that way we shall be able to get something like uniformity right across the country and also that the act and the regulations will be administered in a far more humane and up to date way than they are at the present time.
While I blame the minister, because I believe his policy is a wrong one, yet I realize the difficulties he faces in respect of old age pensions; but I would point out to him, with all the sincerity I can muster, that the Canadian people are very much in earnest over this question of old age pensions, and that now is the time to act.

So much has been said about old age pensions in the many years I have been here that I believe very little can be added to what has been said so well by others. May I add only a few words to what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver South, when he urged so strongly that it is the government's duty to do something now. and to prepare something of a uniform nature. That suggestion I strongly endorse. I do not know where we are going to go in respect of old age pensions .payments, and the regulation of ages, unless something is done at once. To do that I would recommend that the federal government in agreement with the provinces take over the whole business. Let this government take it over entirely. I see no reason why it cannot be done in that way-with provincial agreement of the financial consideration, of course. If that is not done, however, there will be chaos from one end of the country to the other.
I remember that during the last election campaign in Ontario one candidate said that
War Appropriation-Finance

if returned to power he would see that the old age pensions regulations were amended so that they would grant S50 a month at fifty years of age. Another man could have said, just as easily, "If I am elected I will see that the old age pensioner gets $60 a month at forty years of age." Under present circumstances there can be no uniformity, and it will become a question of who is the biggest demagogue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The age will go down and the pension will go up.

Yes, unless the federal government takes over the whole business and arranges something uniform which would apply in every province in exactly the same way. There is no telling where the present method will end.
I thought that on March 13 the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre delivered a very able speech, and one which had required a good deal of thought and care. What he said was well considered, and I must compliment him upon his ability to line up figures one after another. He pointed out-and I am not questioning it-that in no two of the ten authorities in Canada, the nine provinces and the Northwest Territories, are the old age pensions the same. Those figures appear in his speech as reported at page 1407 of Hansard. That being so, there is no uniformity. Therefore I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South when he says that now is the time to do something, and I strongly recommend and suggest that the federal government take over the whole thing. It could easily arrange with the provinces as to where the money is to come from. At the present time it puts up seventy-five per cent. Then, in one province after another we find an addition of five per cent, or this or that, and the result is. that to-day we have no uniformity.
Therefore, to avoid demagogic bidding in general elections, or in provincial elections, to avoid competition between this and that party, to avoid bidding for votes by promising the impossible-because some of these promises are impossible-the federal government should take over the whole thing and make regulations which would be uniformly applicable to all provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. member think that would eliminate the bidding?
It would reduce the bidding from nine bidders, nine provinces, to one bid among the parties in the federal field.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Instead of nine small auctions there would be one big auction, you think?

And the stakes might be even greater.
Mr. MaoNICOL: They are having the same trouble in the United States. It is much more difficult over there to adopt a uniform procedure. They are having difficulty in each and every state, because the various parties in those states are bidding so as to get the pensionable vote. They are offering lower age limits and increased pension payments. Pensions in the United States range from $20 to $50 a month. California pays $50 and Alaska pays $45 a month. In many of the states the age at which the pensioner begins to participate is lower than it is in other states.
I like to see uniformity in these things. For the life of me I cannot see how we are going to get along, either here or in the United States, by following the procedure we have to-day. I find that eight American states pay $40 a month; one pays S36, and the remainder pay somewhere between $20 and $30.
The platforms of the various parties in respect of old age pensions are not far apart, as they have been enunciated in the past few years. I remember that when I first came here in 1930 certain resolutions were presented, chiefly by hon. members who were then associated with labour, I believe. The then hon. member for Winnipeg North, the then hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and later the hon. member for Vancouver East moved resolutions along those lines. Those resolutions were not far apart. At that time I strongly supported the principle of reducing the age limit for old age pensions.
I have had a long association with the working men in the industries with which I have been connected, and I know that with sicknesses and lay-offs and the large families with which God always blesses them-and God uses good judgment in doing bo-most of them find it impossible from their earnings to lay up anything for their old age. That is why I have supported the principle of old age pensions, even before I came to this house. A resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East reads:
Therefore be it resolved, that in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of reducing from seventy years to sixty-five years the age at which the Old Age Pensions Act becomes operative and of increasing the monthly pension at least fifty per cent.
As I recollect, I supported that resolution, although I do not remember whether it came to a vote. That showed that in 1937 the hon. member for Vancouver East advocated that the age limit should be sixty-five years and that the pension should be $30 a month. I

War Appropriation-Finance
have advocated that on many occasions. In 1939 the then hon. member for Winnipeg North, Mr. Heaps, moved a resolution, which read:
Whereas it is becoming more ancl more difficult for older persons to be absorbed into the useful productive life of the dominion, therefore being unable to maintain themselves in decency and comfort;
And whereas Canada is a country richly endowed with natural resources capable of maintaining our whole population in a reasonably high standard of living;
Therefore be it resolved, that this house would welcome a government declaration of policy that would bring about an immediate lowering of the present pensionable age limit of seventy years, the effect of such being that the older generation would retire from industrial activity, thereby creating opportunities for the younger generation to be usefully and gainfully employed.
I presume that resolution meant to lower the age limit to perhaps sixty-five years. While it does not mention that the pension should be increased, I have no doubt that at that time the former hon. member advocated it. He was always most sincere in his efforts for the good of the working man. In making this reference to the former member for Winnipeg North, I am not saying anything against the present member for Winnipeg North.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Perhaps you are mixing up Winnipeg North and Winnipeg North Centre.

I am referring to Mr. Heaps, whatever riding he represented. He was always an ardent advocate of benefits for the working man. What is the situation as far as the Progressive Conservatives are concerned? I take them first because I am a member of that party. At their convention in Winnipeg in 1942 they advocated the payment of an increased old age pension at a reduced age. The present pension is $20 a month, and while I do not know what the framers of that resolution had in mind, I know I have advocated for many years that $1 a day should be given to old age pensioners, which would be approximately $30 a month, and that the age limit should be reduced to sixty-five years. While I cannot interpret just what the party meant at Winnipeg, I am interpreting it to suit myself.
That would be an auction as well.

I stand where I have always stood, namely, that the age limit should not be more than sixty-five years and the amount paid should be not less than $1 a day, or approximately $30 a month. I have
found that in Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand and many states of the United States the pension is paid to women at the age of sixty years. I am in accord with that. Women have a double burden to bear and perhaps they are entitled to an old age pension at an earlier year than the men.
What about the Liberal programme? At the 1942 convention they passed a resolution that the age limit should be reduced. The present limit is seventy years and I presume that they meant to reduce it to sixty-five years although they do not say so. If we assume that they meant sixty-five years, that would bring them on the same platform as I am on. They say in the resolution that the amount of pension should be raised. It is now $20 a month, so that I would interpret the resolution as meaning that they intended to increase the pension to $30 a month or $1 a day. That would place the national Liberal federation or association or perhaps the party on approximately the same footing as myself on that subject.
The Liberal convention of 1942 advocated the dropping of liens. Perhaps there should be some limitation here. It has been advocated that houses valued at $2,000 or $2,500 should be exempt from liens. I believe any humble home should be exempt from a lien, but some of the expensive homes should not be exempt. I would presume that the exemption of a $2,000 or a $2,500 home would have the approval of the Liberal association, although they do not state any amount.
What would happen to the house worth $2,500 upon the death of the pensioner?

If he had a family, it would go to the family. I presume that is what the Liberal federation had in mind in 1942 when they passed the resolution that there should be no lien. My hon. friend was there.

Give him time.

In 1944 the Social Credit party sent out a letter which stated that they advocated the reduction of the age limit to sixty years and an increase in the pension to $50. That was a pretty strong bid for votes, raising the pension to $50.

That was not a bid for votes; that was simply a statement of the bare minimum to which an old age pensioner in Canada is entitled. Anything less than that is an insult.

I notice that the same feeling is quite strong throughout Alberta because I have seen several resolutions from that province, advocating a reduction of the age limit to sixty years and an increase in the pension to $50. The Social Credit programme does not say anything about liens on homes.
In 1942 the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation advocated that the age limit be reduced to sixty years and that the amount of pension be raised to $40 a month. They also advocated that liens against houses should be dropped. I do not remember whether their programme placed a limit of $2,000 or $2,500 on the homes that should be exempt. There was something else that amused me greatly. In the letter of the C.C.F. which sets out their programme in connection with old age pensions and which is signed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), it is stated that in 1927 former members of the labour party, which I presume would refer to the former member for Winnipeg North and per-hape the former member for Winnipeg North Centre, held the balance of power in this house, That is a far-fetched statement.
What did they do about old age pensions while they had the power?

In the parliament elected in 1926 there were 116 Liberals, ninety-one Conservatives, thirteen Progressives, nine Liberal Progressives, three Labour, two, of them from Manitoba, and one Independent; so that if the two Labour members who later became Cooperative Commonwealth supporters held the balance of power-well, I cannot figure that out on these statistics.

To complete the record, would it not be well to recall that the act passed in 1926 was vetoed by the senate, and that the act which went into force was passed in 1927 when the Liberals had a clear majority in the house?

Thank you for the interjection, but I have no comment to make on it at the moment.
Just a word or two further. As I understand it-I may be wrong but this is my understanding-a Canadian who moves to Great Britain and resides there for twelve years becomes eligible for the old age pension there when he reaches the age of sixty-five. But in Canada to become eligible for the old age pension a man or woman must reside here continuously for twenty years. In my riding we have a number of people who have come there from Newfoundland. They are a fine type of citizen, thrifty, hard-working; there

are no better citizens anywhere. A few' years ago, when there was a great demand here for labour and when conditions in the fishing industry in Newfoundland were bad because of certain European conditions, quite a number of Newfoundlanders moved to Canada. They came here in good faith. Now they find themselves handicapped by this residence qualification, requiring twenty years residence in Canada before they can become eligible for the pension. It means that they may have to reach the age of eighty, ciglity-five or ninety years before they will become eligible for the pension here. That is not fair to our brothers from Newfoundland. I can see that unless we make a reciprocal arrangement with Great Britain with respect to the citizens of Great Britain -who leave the homeland prior to being eligible for a pension there and come to Canada, we shall not have that immigration from the old country which we certainly desire very ardently-I do in any event-because if they have to live here for twenty years before they become eligible for the pension they will not leave the fine social conditions they have in the old country. So that I suggest to the government that thej' consider making a reciprocal arrangement with Great Britain whereby a British citizen from the old land will not lose his entitlement to the old age pension at pensionable age by coming to Canada. I think we should also make a similar reciprocal arrangement with Newfoundland, so that we shall treat Newfoundlanders coming to Canada just as if they were Canadians. We want them to be Canadians. But with the present twenty years' residence requirement before they can obtain the old age pension we are penalizing them for coming here to live with us.

Prime Minister's Office Canada
* Ottawa, January 28, 1926.
J. S. Woodsworth, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Woodsworth:
Replying to the letter received from Mr. Heaps and yourself, dated January 7, in which you ask whether it is the intention of the government to introduce at this session legislation with regard to (a) provision for the unemployed, and (b) old age pensions, I would refer you, respecting provision for the unemployed, to the answer given in the House of Commons to-day by the Honourable _ Ernest Lapointe on behalf of the government in reply to a question by yourself, and which indicated the government's intention of carrying out with respect to emergency relief the practice adapted in cooperation with provinces and municipalities in the years immediately following the war. In answer to a question from Mr. Neill, Mr. Lapointe further intimated that it was the intention of the government to introduce at this session legislation with respect to old age pensions.
You will observe that the statement made by Mr. Lapointe was in accordance with the intimation which I gave to Mr. Heaps and yourself at the time of our interview, following the receipt of the communication herein referred to.
With respect to amendments to (a) the Immigration Act, (b) the Naturalization Act, and (c) the criminal code, which were referred to at the time of our interview, I would say that having since taken up the proposed amendments with the ministers concerned, I feel I am in a position to assure you that legislation on these matters will also be introduced in the course of the present session.
Yours sincerely,
In the Prime Minister's handwriting is the signature "W. L. Mackenzie King'". I point out for the record the fact that the letter establishes that immediately after January' 7, which was the opening day of the parliamentary session for that year, there was an interview between Mr. Woodsworth, Mr. Heaps and the Prime Minister, that they discussed the subjects mentioned in this letter, and that the Prime Minister intimated to them that old age pension legislation would be introduced at that session.

It seems to me that every year this question of old age pensions is brought up and discussed by a number of members. On only one or two occasions have I heard, either in this chamber or in committees, anyone objecting to increasing old age pensions. I cannot say it is unanimous, but I can say that almost all agree that old age pensions should be increased, because there are only very, very few-not more than one or two, I should imagine-who are opposed to such increase.
I say that because I am sure that if to-day the minister were to bring in legislation to increase pensions for the aged, and to lower the age at which pensions might be received, or to widen, within reasonable limits, the scope of those eligible to receive them, he would receive the support of almost every member of the house. There would be no difficulty whatsoever. Therefore I am amazed that the minister neglects to do so, because this is a most serious question, especially for those who are concerned.
It should not be considered that we give old age pensions as charity; rather they should be given as of right. And when we think of pensions in that way we must also realize that these old people are deserving. Back through the ages, since Canada's inception, it was they who built up the country. Surely anyone who came here in the old days, who established a homestead, cultivated the soil, and cut down the trees to build up a great section of an empire, should not be denied a decent standard of living.
If it is a question of finance, of course that is a different matter, and one which we should be discussing. I venture to say, however, that the Minister of Finance would not offer that as a reason. Surely we have reached the time, after having spent so many billions of dollars for war, when there can be no further question about raising money to increase old age pensions, especially to that level where it is possible for the pensioners to keep body and soul together.
Some may say that the pensioners are getting along all right now. I heard one or two hon. members say that, but it is not so. On the amount of pension the old age pensioners are getting to-day-$20 a month, until the other $5 was added, making a present total of $25-what standard of living can they have? I venture to say the minister himself could not get along very far on $25 a month. If he had to maintain a home, or a room, buy his clothes and feed himself on $25 a

The hon. member for Davenport referred to the resolution which was passed in the Alberta legislature recommending a pension of $50 a month to be paid at the age of sixty years. There was a suggestion that that was done for political purposes, but I would remind him that Alberta is one of the provinces which have taken the lead in increasing old age pensions and trying to make living conditions of the older people a little better. That has been its attitude since 1935 when it was first elected. It did not wait to have this matter brought up as political propaganda. I would not even suggest that the minister brought down the orders in council referring to old age pensions for political purposes, although the Saskatchewan election may not be very far off. I know that was not the purpose at all in regard to Alberta. That would be too small a thing to do, to trifle with the incomes of these older people for such purposes as that.
Another aspect of this matter which was referred to in the statement made by the minister is the contributory scheme of old age pension. I want to say at once that I am against a contributory form of old age pension; I think it should be non-contributory. It should be given to these people as a right, not as a charity. As is suggested, they have given their lives to this country and when you have done that you cannot do more. I think it is wrong to talk about contributory old age pensions. There are many angles that could be discussed in regard to contributory or noncontributory old age pensions, but no doubt that subject will come up in the social security committee when we finish dealing with the health insurance bill. In view of the legislative programme before us and the rate of progress we have made lately, it is not likely that w.e shall get through with these matters this session. I have no great hope that the

question of old age pensions will be settled this summer, and that is why I am somewhat concerned. When the minister brought down these orders in council he should have brought them down in a form which would have provided better conditions for these older people.
There are some things in the orders that are worth while, but it must be remembered that the pension is not increased. All that has been done is to increase the amount of income which a pensioner may have from outside sources over and above his allowable pension, and this has been increased to the extent of $60 a year or $5 a month. That does not represent a very substantial increase. It works out to about eighteen per cent, the increase in the cost of living index. I think everyone in the committee will agree that the cost of living has increased more than eighteen per cent. The index is based only on the necessities of life; the general standard of living has increased much more than that. This small increase of $60 a year or $5 a month provided by the order in council will not pay the increased cost of living which these older people have been compelled to pay since the war started. I think the change in the resident qualifications is worth while; that is the sixteen years requirement between the ages of fifty and seventy years. I think it was suggested this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that there should be some change in the period from fifty to seventy years.
The clause in the order in council providing for movement from one province to another is a good one, as is the clause which provides for service on ships or in the fishing industry. I am not going to discuss this matter at great length to-night since I have spoken on it before and I assume it will come up in the social security committee. However, I am very much disappointed that the order in council did not provide for a greater increase. I suppose the minister had in mind that later on there would be other legislation brought down, probably after the report of the social security committee was presented, which would in effect raise the actual amount given to old age pensioners. I am sure we would all agree with that.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to review the details of the old age pension system in Canada because they are fairly well known to all members of the committee, but I should like to bring to the attention of the committee a phase of the old age pension system which I think is a peculiar and unique development of the present war. Without referring to it in detail, may I say that one of the warnings given to parliament and to the government by the governor of the Bank of

Canada deals with a phase of our post-war adjustment that must be known to every member of this House of Commons who is conversant with the revolutionary development that has taken place in the last four years in Canada's power to produce.
One of the great problems that we are going to face-and it is not peculiar to the factory but applies just as well to the farm-will be to find the means to absorb and consume the enormous quantity of consumer goods that we can produce with comparative ease, and with the employment of a smaller proportion of wagearners than would have been required to produce the same volume of goods before the war. I believe that we should recognize our old age pension system as a potent factor-not by any means the whole solution-by which we can increase consumption and at the same time relieve the pressure of competition among the wagearners producing consumer goods. To some people that may seem a mug's game, as we heard in the banking and commerce committee the other day.
What does that mean?
If you ever gave any money away and awaikened one day to the fact that you were not going to get it back, you would be playing what some people would call a mug's game.
I never heard the expression before.
It is a very old English expression. It is the adoption of that kind of economy where you cast your bread upon the waters without any hope of its ever returning.
I have often done that.

But I am not speaking about any mug's game. I am speaking about a sound, practical innovation in the economic life of the Dominion of Canada. Of course I thoroughly disagree with the continuance of the old age pension administration in the Department of Finance. The Minister of Finance cannot serve two masters. In the very nature of things he wants to keep his expenditures as low as possible; he wants to keep his burden of taxation as light as possible; and when he is called upon to face those responsibilities, who is apt to suffer if he is at one and the same time the representative of the taxpayer and the representative of the old age pensioner? We want a man representing the old age pensioners in Canada

who will fight with the Minister of Finance for more for the old age pensioners-and I cannot see the Minister of Finance fighting with himself for the old age pensioner.
This is a rebellion, Mr. Chairman.
That is one of the privileges we have in the Liberal party.
You will find out if you go far enough. They do not tolerate rebellion over there.
They have stood me for a long time and I have not changed much in the seven years I have been here.
But the times are getting rough.

What I am advocating is a change in attitude, and I believe that in the change in attitude that should come with regard to old age pensions will be found something of the fundamental principle that we must employ if we are actually going to win the peace and establish expanding progress and expanding security with growing prosperity. Will anybody in this house qr in the Department of Finance or elsewhere say that we in Canada cannot provide our old age pensioners with all the food they need? Is there anybody who can say that we are unable to provide them with all the clothing they need? Is there anybody who will say that we cannot provide them with a house fittingly comfortable for an aged Canadian? We have all these things in abundance. Is there anybody who will say that a man who has come to the age of retirement is not entitled to a radio and some of the comforts of this earth as well as the bare necessities of life?
A picture show, for instance, once in a while?

Yes, and he should not have to borrow money at 9| per cent for medical services either. If it is true, then, that we have an abundance of the things that are necessary to sustain life, upon what principle will the men of this parliament support a Department of Finance that demands for our old age pensioners in Canada life on the basis of pauperism? That day must come to an end.
And now is a good time.

The day when we place human values and human considerations above money will be the day when we shall have the peace that our men are fighting and dying for to-night. The whole attitude of finance
to the old age pensioners discloses the wholly false attitude of the financial institutions in our whole economy. I know it was very popular a few years ago for men to declare that the. granting of any form of old age pension would destroy the character of the individual, would destroy thrift, would break down the morale of our people. Let me refer the committee to one man's attitude wTith regard to that. I should like to place on the record a few remarks made by the present Prime Minister of Great Britain, in a speech made by Winston. Churchill when he was the flaming crusader of Liberalism in Dundee in 1908. He said:
We are told that our non-contributory scheme of old age pensions, for instance, will be fatal to thrift, and we are warned that the great mass of the working classes will be discouraged thereby from making any effective provision for their old age. But what effective provision have they made against old age in the past? If terror be an incentive to thrift, surely the penalties of the system which we have abandoned ought to have stimulated thrift as much as anything could have been stimulated in this world. The mass of the labouring poor have known that unless they made provision for their old age betimes, they_ would perish miserably in the workhouse. Yet they have made no provision; and when I am told that the institution of old age pensions will prevent the working classes from making provision for their old age, I say that cannot be, for they have never been able to make such provision. And I believe our scheme, so far from preventing thrift, will encourage it to an extent never before known. It is a great mistake to suppose that thrift is caused only by fear. It springs from hope as well as from fear, and where there is no hope be sure there will be no thrift.
Those men who in their own strength can go and take care of themselves, who believe in the ruthless philosophy of "root hog or die" and never had a bit of compassion in their souls, could have taken a lesson long ago in the Canadian parliament from the words of Winston Churchill, uttered in 1908. And when he beoame chancellor of the British exchequer in 1925 he rationalized and improved the old age pension system to a great degree.
The man who believes that the old age pensioner is a liability to the state and the taxpayer is unsound in his economic philosophy. If you give to the old age pensioners of Canada means of living upon a decent standard whom do they employ? They employ the farmer who produces the food, who has had surpluses in the past and, when the war markets go, will have surpluses again. Yes, our fruit will be rotting on the field and all the things which the farmer produces will be begging for consumers within a very short period of time after this war is over. Are we then going to stand forth and say that in the midst of this abundance there shall be' starvation and misery again? Let us change
