our hearts and look upon this principle, not through the eyes of the money-changer and the money-lender, but through the eyes of common sense, guided by the plainest and simplest of humanitarian motives, and we shall be ashamed to stand up and admit to the condition of the old age pensioner imposed by a federal law.
Now, Churchill recognized that, and in 1909 he made another speech, when he had this to say:
But there is another issue which must not be overlooked. I mean the social issue. We have taken a great step already. I must say that he is a rather sour kind of man who can find nothing to notice in the old age pensions act except its little flaws and petty defects. I think you will feel on the other hand, that the establishment of the pensions system is a marvellous and impressive example of the power which British governments possess. Without a hitch, perfectly smoothly, punctual to the minute, regular as clockwork, nearly six hundred thousand aged persons are being paid .their pensions every week. That is a wonderful and beneficent achievement, a good job well worth some risk and sweat to finish. Nearly eight millions of money are being sent circulating through unusual channels, long frozen :by poverty, circulating in the homes of the .poor, flowing through the little shops which cater to their needs, cementing again family unions which harsh fate was tearing asunder, uniting the wife to the husband, and the parent to the children. No; in spite of socialistic sneer and Tory jeer and glorious beer, and all the rest of it, I say it is a noble and inspiring event, for which this parliament will he justly honoured by generations unborn.
Look at the England of to-day; look at what she has stood to, and ask yourself if the inauguration of the old age pension system and its steady improvement have ever undermined the character, the thrift or the courage of the English-speaking race. It has been a help and a power in building a stronger and a better nation.

It is true that there were a great many people all across the Dominion of Canada advocating the establishment of the old age pension system. It is true that some correspondence passed between certain members in the independent ranks and the Prime Minister. And this fact remains: the bill which was passed in 1926 was vetoed in the senate.

What I want to bring particularly to the attention of the minister is the Liberal policy on old age pensions as declared by the Prime Minister in 1931. He laid down these principles for the guidance of Liberalism, and I have never known our leader to change his attitude in that regard:
The Liberal administration fought for many years for an old age pensions act, and care I think was taken to make it clear that an amendment to the British North America Act would be required before this federal government would have power to administer an old age pension scheme. It was recognized that an amendment to the British North America Act would take some time, and for that reason the government of the day adopted the method of agreeing to give those grants in aid to the provinces on condition that they would carry out a scheme framed by the federal government which would be similar in all the provinces.
An hon. Member: A vicious principle.
Mr. Mackenzie King: The principle, from a financial point of view, was unsound. I am quite prepared to concede that. But I will go a step further and say that,' in my opinion, this parliament ought to remedy the unsoundness of the principle, not by discontinuing to vote money for old age pensions, but by assuming the entire obligation, one hundred per cent. This government should take over the whole scheme and itself pay out the money. That is the position that should foe taken; that is the proper way to remedy what there is of unsoundness in the principle. . . .
Obviously the principle is thoroughly sound. I have always taken that position and have fought strenuously for it; and to get that principle recognized by parliament, I was prepared to go so far as to support a grant in aid, which I am perfectly frank to admit was, from the point of view of financing, an unsound method. Now I say, let us recognize that the principle of old age pensions itself is perfectly sound and involves an obligation which the federal parliament should assume. Let us undertake to administer the Old Age Pensions Act from Ottawa and have all the moneys which are necessary for the payment of those pensions voted by this parliament.
Here we have a declaration of principle by the present Prime Minister; we have his government in power; and for some reason there are forces within this government that refuse to follow the declared principles of our leader and refuse to recognize the stand that
we as Liberals have taken all down history, of giving to our old age pensioners something that every Canadian can be proud of.
I plead with the Minister of Finance-and this may be the last session of this parliament before the reconstruction period arrives: Let us leave upon the records a national old age pension system which will treat our old age people in Canada, in need, as economic units of consuming value. Let us treat them as people who are retiring from the competition of employment, and let us out of that great richness which we own in Canada put to the practical test the kind of thing we talk so much about and rarely put into practice.
That is good.
Yes; it is good.
It is quite true, too.

One of the sad things about our whole economy is that we who are secure, we who have been gifted with the intelligence and the strength and in some instances the good fortune to establish ourselves in sheltered positions of security, have too little thought for those less fortunate than ourselves. When in that other place the old age pension was vetoed I often thought it strange as coming from such an assembly, secure with a salary for life, comfortably ensconced, with transportation provided, that they should look upon the aged of the land as entitled to get but a mere $20 a month after reaching the age of seventy, when all good Christians are supposed to be dead, while in that place, in all its security, that proposal was vetoed, depriving the Canadian in need, over seventy years of age, of a mere pittance of 820 a month. And on what grounds? On the very grounds which our present Minister of Finance offered in the last session of this parliament. It would cost too much. It should be contributory. It would destroy the thrift and character of the Canadian people. And yet, mark you, the people of this country are not going to forget that we were rich enough to lend to Britain 8700,000,000 and to produce and give to this war effort a billion dollars worth of goods, over our own goods and services, and that we stood in this house and defended our chartered banking system putting away in reserves, hidden and otherwise, tens and tens o'f millions of dollars. Yes, we found in that banking system men pensioned at the age of sixty-five; and if we Liberals think we can find endorsement from the electors of Canada, after giving evidence of being the richest people in the world, when we cannot do better for our old age pensioners than we are doing, then I think

we shall find that not only the old age pensioners but a great army of men and women who are awakening to this injustice will let us know that they do not approve our attitude.
I say this as a warning. While I realize that the Liberal party has some defects, I can see no hope over there, and less in the far corner opposite.
That is where you are wrong. The only people who have the courage of their convictions are right over here.

That is the trouble; they have too much courage. I have seen what happens to people right within your own party, because they do not agree with you- and I know the fate of Mr. Trotsky. I know that if I ever had to contend with that kind of thing and yo-ur group came into power I would be one of those fellows who would talk as freely then as I talk now, and I do not know what the end of me would be. I am worried about that. I am afraid I would hit a salt mine or a concentration camp.
Mr. GILLIS; We will do the things you are talking about.

I have a great deal of sympathy for my hon. friends in that regard and I think the majority of men in the Liberal party would do it; and if we had you fellows over here on our side, and a lot of the Tories in the Liberal party out of this party, we would all be able to do it together.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Do you not have the majority rule in the Liberal party?
What about Tim Buck?
There are some of us-and we do not mind saying so now-who have that feeling, and we expect the Liberal party to be true to Liberalism.
Whatever that is.
If it is, it will not be trailing behind other countries in the matter of old age pensions and social services; it will be leading them.
Vain hope.

One of the charges made against the countries of the British empire is that we possess too much of this world's wealth and use it too little, and there is no part of the British empire where that charge can be made with greater justification than right here in Canada. One of the reasons why we have failed to give our people the abundance that we are capable of producing is that we have been afraid to put buying power

into their hands. Now we are to be told, I suppose, that if we gave the old age pensioners a decent standard of living, that would cause inflation.
I guess so.

Well, that nonsense will not go with the people of Canada any longer. We were told that kind of nonsense back in the days of the depression, in the days of 1936, 1937, 1938, and 1939. The Canadian people will not accept from any government the declaration that we cannot find the money to give our old age pensioners a decent standard of living after the record we have established in finding the billions we have found to carry on a successful war effort, and not out of taxation, not out of borrowing, but out of the printing of Bank of Canada bills, and the creation of new money by allowing our bankers to use pen and ink to write up their own bank deposits. I had hoped after the last session of parliament that there would be some changes in this system, but I wish to say.that it is with sincere and deep regret I find our Department of Finance just as much against the old age pensioner to-day as they were when after a long struggle and on the eve of the Ontario election we were able to wrest from the Department of Finance a meagre $5 a month increase with no increase in the total amount for the year.
They are putting it off now until the eve of the next election.

Those orders in council that have been read and this statement that has been made passing the buck to the provincial governments will not be accepted by the Canadian people either. There is, in addition to that, the indifference to the old age pensioner. It is said that if we provide contributory old age pensions on a decent standard and pensions for those who have never had an opportunity to contribute as voluntary old age pensioners a lot of insurance companies believe that it will cut down the number of insurance policies that will be held by the Canadian people. One of the real obstacles-and the Canadian people have to come to know this- is. the organized power of resistance to the establishment of the right kind of social services, the right kind of old age pensions. Why do not we amend our Unemployment Insurance Act and provide in that act that when a man has paid in to it for a certain length of time he will be allowed to retire and move out of competition in the production of consumer goods? All industrial activities that have pen-

IFor Appropriation-Finance
sion schemes do that. Our banks do it. Why do not we or the government do it? Where is the resistance?
I hope that before this parliament prorogues some steps will be taken to place the old age pensioners of Canada on a much higher plane of living than they are now placed and that the age limit will be reduced from seventy to sixty-five for men and from seventy to sixty for women. I ask consideration for this not merely upon humanitarian grounds but also upon the sound basis that it is one place where we can safely put consumer buying into circulation without fear of inflation and as a means of creating employment for those who have to find employment producing consumer goods and services for others.

I am sorry that I cannot rise to the heights of histrionic ability shown by the last speaker in discussing this matter; I also regret that I have been otherwise engaged and have not my notes on this subject as coherent as they should be; but I wish to touch on two or three points where at least I shall have the advantage, of knowing thoroughly the subjects on which I wish to talk, having been actually present on the occasion. I shall also try to treat it in a practical and realistic way.
I have a suggestion to make to the Minister of Finance which I think, if it had been suggested earlier and acted upon, would have saved a great deal of the time of this house which I think we are all trying to do.
Why does he not-it is not too late yet because heaven knows how much longer this debate is going to take-send this subject to the committee appointed for many years past to deal specifically with such matters? This committee is called the industrial and international relations committee. I have been on it ever since I have been here. It has not sat for the last seven years. I am not sure whether it is seven or four years. There are two committees, one of which has not sat for seven years and the other for four. The industrial and international relations committee is set up specially to deal with such subjects. The matter of old age pensions was brought up in that committee long before I was here; in 1912 or 1914, I forget which. It reached the usual report of a partisan committee but it served to start the subject. If I remember rightly it was brought up again in 1919, also when I was not here. They made a little more progress; they showed a little more zeal, so to speak, and the matter was again stalled by bringing in a vague report with the government doing nothing on it. Then I came into the house in 1921 and I
began in 1922, which was the first session, to agitate for this matter. We had a committee which discussed it for two years running. At the first year's committee we discussed the question at great length; I think we put in a report to the effect that we discovered or realized that according to the British North America Act it was a provincial responsibility, and that we could only proceed along the lines of helping out, but could not attempt to run things without a change in the act, and we suggested that the provinces should be invited to express their intention as to how far they would go and what assistance they would require. We obtained that information during the recess, and again in the next year, which I think was 1924, we brought in a definite recommendation that the government should bring in an old age pension act. It simmered along and nothing was done. An election was held in 1925. I might take a minute here to explain the difference between the last speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, and the hon. member for York-Sunbury. As often happens when two men are flatly contradicting each other, there is a certain amount of truth on both sides, but misunderstanding.
What happened was this: an election was held in the fall of 1925. The hon. member for York-Sunbury said that the Liberals came back with ninety-one members.
A hundred and one.

No man can deny me this,
because I have the red book Parliamentary Guide before me. I am talking about the election of 1925, not 1926. Here it is in the Canadian Parliamentary Guide. In the election of 1925 the Liberals came back with a total of 101.
Quite right.

The hon. member for York-Sunbury is right. That was not a majority, but the Liberals had a slight majority because there was always a certain number of people who did not want an election and so on. The government went along for a few months. Then, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury said, they made a deal, a quite proper deal, with two or three members to give them support for one term, I think it was, on condition that an old age pension measure be brought down. The Prime Minister of the day adhered to his agreement; we adhered to ours and the bill was brought down.

They put the gun to his head.

Now, give a man a chance. That was the election of 1925. The government made this deal and they introduced the

Old Age Pensions Act in 1926.. They put it through, and it was an excellent bill. The government by that time had found they could not get the provinces to do anything anyway. The provinces wanted the dominion to do it, and they shilly-shallied, and would not do one thing or another. The government, to its credit, said, "We will do it. There is only one way we can do it, and that is this way: we will pass what the lawyers call an enabling act. It will show that we are willing to give fifty per cent of a certain sum. Here is a draft bill. If you-Ontario, Manitoba and all the rest of the provinces, or any of them- want the pension, we will pay fifty per cent." But they did not bring it into effect immediately, because it had to pass the provinces. We had to get their consent. I am intensely sorry to have to disagree with my new-found sponsor the hon. member for York-Sunbury. and tell him he was mistaken when he said that his party had endorsed it, because I can remember the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen saying, "There will not be a dollar paid under this act; fraud is written in every line."
That was said about the first bill. That bill was sent to the senate, and the senate killed it. Then the government was defeated on another measure altogether. They went to the country, and the old age pensions proved to be remarkably and unusually popular. The government got into power, largely because of that, perhaps, and they put the same bill through, identically the same bill. Then the senate took the view that the country had pronounced upon it, and let it go through. On that occasion it is only right to say that the Conservative party certainly did not vote against the second passing of the bill. So that the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard is right when he says that the Liberal party, with a sufficient majority behind them, did not have to make a bargain with anybody. On the other hand, the Conservative party did not oppose it the second time it was passed.
I have to answer the hon. member for York-Sunbury with respect to the election of 1926. He said the Liberals only got 116 members; that is true. But the Conservative party got only ninety-one. But the Liberal party could count upon a number of Progressives-thirteen, I believe, and nine Liberal Progressives, and occasionally they could pull in the U.F.A. from Alberta. The government had sufficient majority to go ahead. The bill went through, and they got the credit for it. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard is right when he says that the Liberal party passed it when
they did not have to. And the Conservative party can say they did not oppose it the second time it was introduced.
I should like to say a word to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who read a letter this afternoon, to which he appeared to attach great importance, so much importance that the blamed thing has been subject to some form of glorification, and has been framed. I do not know whether it is printed or embossed, but it is no doubt considered as the last word in political strategy. I have no doubt it will be playing an important part in the election in Saskatchewan within the next two weeks.

speech which was worth framing. However, the hon. member quoted a letter from the Prime Minister. It was written in language considered to be confidential, and never intended to be blatted forth. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I heard him say that, myself. I heard Mr. Woodsworth say at a meeting in Courtenay, before a Rotary club, that he gave

me great credit for my action in helping to get the old age pension measure passed. There is plenty of credit for both of us. I gave him due credit, and he gave me due credit. But hon. members to my left now hog it all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No one is taking it. I read the letter, and your name appeared in it.
It is not such a credit.
I am quite willing to give credit where credit is due. Does not Scripture say "Agree with thine adversary quickly lest he turn and rend thee."
Or stab you in the back.

With respect to the committee I was going to say that it recommended a resolution which afterwards became law at a very important and long session. Representatives of all parties were on the committee. Witnesses from far and wide were called. We always asked them two questions: What do you think the age should be? What do you think the minimum amount should be? I remember that a railway man, a very intelligent man, representing one of the railway unions, said, "That does not interest us because we will have to help pay for it; we have our own pension scheme, but I would say to you to go ahead and get it passed; do not quibble about the amount; it would be better to get it passed if you only get $20, because public sentiment will see that it is increased; but get it passed." I thought that was very sound advice. When it came to deciding upon that section of the report which prescribed the amount we were distinctly told, not only by the government of the day but by every representative of the different parties in the house, publicly and privately, that we had not a ghost's chance to get it through if we asked for more than $20. I will take my bible oath that that was the situation.
One gentleman who is now a leading light in the C.C.F. party, who is an organizer, I do not know whether of all Canada or of Alberta only, got up and said, "I propose that it be $40." I said to him, "Mr. So-and-so"-I will not say who it is for the sake of his unborn children-"what do you think is the best thing to do; do you think it is better to hold out for $40 and get turned down, as you know and cannot deny will be the fate of this measure, or to take some lesser amount, say $20, and regard it as a stepping-stone to something higher, as being of some advantage for these old people?" He said, "I would rather ask for $40 and get turned down, for I would get the credit in the country." Even in those days-there were no C.C.F. then; but
[.Mr. Neill.]
he had the same desires-he was ready to sell
out the interests of the old people for a place of profit, for a chance to advance to power by just one little bit. That is what is going on to-day. That is not carrying out the principles of government; it is just expediency.

the best he could.

May I ask a question with respect to Mr. Meighen? The hon. member said that Mr. Meighen based his appeal on fraud. Mr. Meighen based his objection at that time on the known fact that under the constitution we had no right to do it, and he charged the Prime Minister with knowing that and still putting the bill through. It was on that basis that it was considered fraudulent.
That is right.
That is the answer.
That may have been his argument.
That was kis argument and that was true in law and in fact.

Then you are on the horns of a dilemma. You have either to say that he wanted to reject a good measure, or that as a lawyer he said it .was constitutionally rotten when it was not. It was afterwards passed and became law in the same exact language.
It was only passed as-
You have to take it one way or the other.
It was only a grant in aid and it is yet.

The bill was passed and it was a good bill. With one exception there has never been any need to change it. Where the mischief was done was in the regulations.

The government in their wisdom passed the power to make regulations over to the provinces and they passed such regulations which, if it were not unparliamentary, I would say were entirely damnable. If that word is improper, I will say they were utterly unworthy of a Christian country.
But that power was given to the wretched little boards in the provinces. I speak more particularly of the one in my own province. They simply made the law unto themselves. If you told them, "This is wrong; this is not the way the act reads," they simply pointed to the section which gave them the power to make regulations. Having that power to make regulations, they made a new act. If, as I pointed out, you said, "You cannot do that; that is contrary to the law," they said, "No; we have the power to make regulations; we can make any regulations we like." And they did. Some of the fool things they did were laughed out of court.
As I pointed out in this house a few years ago, there were a number of questions, I think about thirty-five, which were asked of applicants for pensions. One question asked was: "Since the old age pension law came into effect"-which was seventeen years before -"have you sold or given away any personal property?" There were some more legal words to the question. An old woman might have had a stove which was worn out and which she had given to her next-door neighbour who was' worse off than she. Then the person to whom she sold it, if she sold it, or the person to whom she had given it, if she had given it away, had to be dug up whether he was in heaven or in California and asked to sign a statement as to the consideration that had passed on that occasion and what had been done with the money. It was not a question of bonds or land; it was simply a question of personal property. Finally something like shame struck the British Columbia board and that was changed to five years. They are still asked what they have done with an old ' saucepan or coal shovel, what they got for it, and they must produce evidence to show it was paid for or, if anything remains unpaid, how much it is. There were a whole lot of rules like that. Probably the government is not responsible for those rules except that it should have taken those people and knocked their heads together.
This government agreed to those regulations.

It sanctioned them.
Another regulation that I object to is that governing the estimated value of property. That is, they take the assessed value of the property, which in British Columbia is
absurdly and ridiculously above the real value.
I would cheerfully sell any of my property for the assessed value. I used to point that regulation out to the government and finally got it changed to either the assessed value or the market value, whichever seemed the more equitable. A man might have a hundred or two hundred acres of useless bushland and five per cent of the assessed value of that land would be considered as income.
What did this board do? They said, "We will continue to adhere to the assessed value." I said, "You cannot; the law has been changed; the regulations have been changed; you should take the market value of this property." I offered to take them from the nearest port in my car to show them the wretched land, but they said, "No; we will take the assessed value." I said: "You cannot; you are going against the law." They said, "We have the option to take whichever we like and we find that taking the assessed value is less trouble to us. We assume the assessors are honest and reliable men." The}' still take the assessed value because it is a little less trouble.
I have known of cases where a woman had 160 acres away back of beyond, away up on the northern edge of Vancouver island. I could not say what it was worth, because it was not worth anything. She might be paying $10 or $12 taxes. She was paying the taxes but getting nothing. But the board said that the property was assessed at, say $1,500 and that five per cent of that would be $75 and they considered that sum as part of the. woman's income. They took five per cent of land that was not worth a curse, land upon which the woman had to pay taxes. I advised this particular owner to sell it, but it could not be sold. I said, "I will give you $10 for it, and then they can charge you only on the $10." That is the sort of thing we had to do to get an honest break for some of these people.
I wish to say just a word or two before I pass away from this. I have been slamming the provincial government. The board was rotten, lock, stock and barrel, but the system has been changed. They have now a new board. I think it was the hon. member for Vancouver South who said pensions ought to be run by a welfare department. It is run now by a welfare department in British Columbia; they have a competent man at the head, and it is to his credit that we are now able to get an old age pension out there much more readily. Very often it was a matter of months and months. I know of one man's case when it took exactly nine months, and then the pension was granted

War Appropriation-Finance
in the end. They were writing to a man who got mail only once a month and the final delay was over his position and earnings. They said: "You are a postmaster and no doubt get a princely recompense, so that we want a certificate signed by someone in authority telling us how much you got every year out of this valuable position." The man finally lost his patience-he had nothing else to lose, and so he wrote back, "Do you want a letter from the postmaster general or from the governor general or from the Prime Minister? There is a blue-book on your table, or ought to be, which will show you that I drew every year the sum of $100." That man had to go without the old age pension for months until they got a certificate that he drew only $100 a year. I know of another man whose pension was held up for months because they could not get a translation of his birth certificate. They could have got it in Vancouver for fifty cents. I have done it.
Another man who applied for an old age pension was dying of cancer. The authorities were holding his pension up until finally I told them, "Give this man his pension or he' will be dead, and then you will be able to say that you saved the government $20 for a month." This man got his pension the day before he died. They wrote him a letter like this, "We know you are very ill. If you are dead when you get this cheque, it must be sent back at once."
I will give the provincial government credit that the system is much better now. It is run by a man who has some human sympathy, who believes in fair dealing, but still handicapped by fool rules.
There is one question I will take up with the minister. I asked him about it last year when this last $5 was added to the pension, and paid for out of the war appropriation. I asked the minister if the $5 would be stopped when the war ended and the minister replied, "Yes, unless legislative action is taken at that time or in the meantime." I hope the minister will take action now by an amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act so that there will be no doubt that the $5 will be continued after the war, so that these pensioners will not be shivering at the thought that, when the war is over, this last $5 that was added to their pension will be taken away again.
Many proposals have been made by hon. members looking to the future. No doubt a contributory system must be brought in at some time in the future and the age limit reduced, but we are living to-day and we have to deal with these people now. I think the hon. member for Vancouver South in his fine speech might have given the government a

little more praise for the action it has taken. There is an old proverb that you should not look a gift horse in the mouth, which means that if a man gives you a present of a horse, do not open its mouth to examine its teeth which tell you the horse's age, because then you might find that he had given you a lemon instead of a horse. The present old age pension is a gift horse. It is an improvement, and I am willing to give the government credit for it. If somebody gives you something, grab it and use it as a stepping-stone to get some further advantage for the people you represent. Do not sneer at it because it is not all that you want and say that it was forced out of the giver. That is not the way to get things. It is the way to choke off at the source anything further of the kind.
I would suggest that the whole question of old age pensions go to a committee. These are local matters which could best be dealt with a committee. The government have a large majority in the house and they would have a majority on the committee. We have dealt with the matter four times already in committee and good came out of every one of those committees. This is not the place to dispute about these small matters. If the minister could see his way to sending the question to the industrial and international relations committee, the whole thing could be threshed out there and amendments suggested, and it would help to popularize the scheme with the people.
Here we are in the midst of a war and I know the large expenditures which the minister is called upon to make. I agree to some extent with the position he takes. I also admit that whenever he proposes to raise the pension, it is not his word alone that goes because he has to get the consent of nine provinces. If he would send the matter to a committee everyone would have an opportunity to be heard; the minister would get a sound basis for future action, post-war, and proposals would be made to deal with the matter equitably in the meantime. It is not just a question of a dollar or two more that irks the old age pensioner. It is the injustice, such as has been done in the cases to which I have referred, and I could go on reciting similar cases for an hour. It is that which kills the spirit of the poor. All question of charity, of course, will be removed in any contributory system, but that cannot be adopted in a moment. I do trust that the minister will accept the suggestion 1 have made.

War Appropriation-Finance

In discussing this vote for old age pensions I shall leave politics out entirely. I was head of the Union of Canadian Municipalities for three years and head of the Ontario Municipal Association for three or four years. I was also a member of the committee on old age pensions, and during the time I sat on the committee I was ashamed of Canada, a so-called Christian country, in its treatment of our aged people or the blind. There is an old saying, "he that hath pity on the poor, lendeth unto the Lord." But for years we could get nothing for our aged people. I was the head of a very large municipality which pioneered in social reform services. The city of Toronto led the dominion in many forms of social legislation and had pension funds for its employees in most departments. We came here on many occasions to interview governments of all kinds and we got very cold and chilly receptions in all forms of aid. The first duty of the government is to look after the health, wealth, happiness and prosperity of its citizens.
This question is not a provincial one. We have the most complicated constitution in the world for the protection of human values in Canada. It is no wonder that juries of all kinds in their reports to the presiding judge have criticized the federal parliament and all governments for years for their utter lack of any Christian charity toward the aged and the poor of this country. It is disgraceful that this debate should have been precipitated in this chamber to-night, with a war on. There has been quarrelling about who did this and who did that, when as a matter of fact not a thing was done until recently for the aged, the blind and the suffering. It was left in the past very largely to the municipalities and private sources. Finally the federal government contributed seventy-five per cent and the provinces twenty-five per cent to the old age pensions. Then on July 24 of last year the maximum pension was raised by this government from $20 to $25 a month, but no cost of living bonus was granted. Where can you get a house for $20 or $25? That will not even buy your food, let alone a room.
We have heard from the British Columbia members to-night, and we are always glad to hear from them. When any question of importance to their province comes up they make, to borrow a phrase from hockey, a ganging attack upon the government. I wish the Ontario members would do the same for their problems.
The Liberals in their platform of 1919 had a scheme for unemployment insurance, sickness and health insurance, but it took them down to a couple of years ago to put such a measure
on the statute book. The first day I was in the house in 1922, I had, with a former member for Winnipeg North Centre, a resolution in favour of sickness, unemployment and health insurance, and in addition, old age pensions for the blind and the aged. This whole problem has been left to the municipalities largely, until lately by the government, excepting for pin-money, for it is really nothing more, handed out in the form of grants of $5 and $10 to those who have borne the burden and heat of the day. It has been a disgraceful manner of dealing with a federal problem, which should be an entirely federal responsibility and not a tax on the municipalities and on real estate.
Just think of the way in which some of our citizens have been used. Long ago, at the time of the rebellion of 1885 in the Northwest Territories, troops from Quebec, Ontario and the maritimes. in response to the country's call, marched across lake Superior in the winter when it was thirty or forty degrees below zero. In those days and from then onwards these men of the militia have done much to build up our armed forces. Yet these 1885 veterans, the backbone of the militia, have never received any pension. We would have had no troops in South Africa and our efforts in the first great war and the present war would have fallen short of what they have been, but for the pioneers in the militia and cadet services of those days. Why have these aged men been used in this fashion? They have experienced the same sort of treatment as the schoolteachers who were allowed to starve in the country school-houses, receiving no more than three or four hundred dollars a year for their services as compared with the way Canada helped the builders of railways. The militia men got a grant of 200 acres, and that was all. To this day some of the 1885 veterans are in the poorhouse, and there they will continue to be, if we wait for Canada.
We tried to get their case discussed in this chamber, but were unable to persuade a so-called Liberal government of the justice of compensating these pioneers and veterans who served us in the northwest rebellion. My leader here and the hon. member for Kootenay West tried to get the matter discussed, but they never were able to have it dealt with.
As regards the blind, little or nothing has been done for them. They have been mainly dependent on the splendid Association for the Blind, upon the municipalities, private persons, the community clubs, and voluntary social agencies, much as are the poor unem-
War Appropriation-Finance

ployed people who found themselves out of work through some of the policies which have prevailed in this country.
What has been done about income tax? What encouragement has been given to those who tried to help in maintaining some of their poorer neighbours, or relatives or those who have contributed in large or small measure to charitable organizations? The charges required of them under the War Measures Act, in the form of income tax, are such as should not exist in any Christian country.
I ask that some consideration be given to these questions. Very little has been done for the pioneers. They are allowed $20 or $25 a month, plus a $5 raise by a province here and there. It is just charity, and charity in its worst form. Those who have worked honourably and well until they are sixty-five or seventy years of age should have a better outlook in life than they get now, namely an open door to a house of industry, or even to a gaol, or a poor-house. At times in the past the gaols have been filled with these poor people. I know, because I have been a municipal officer for many years, and have always taken great interest in social problems. Yet the parliament of Canada was able to vote millions of dollars for branch lines and other material purposes, while it could not treat with reasonable generoshy builders of character in the schools and the poor old folks. But as for the builders of railways, they were presented with the title deeds of the country.
We have been a long way behind other countries in legislation for social purposes. Let me tell the last two speakers, although I have great respect for them because they usually contribute matters of interest to debates in which they take part, that on this question they cannot afford to adopt a holier-than-thou attitude. Here we can afford $140 million to support ceilings some of which may collapse overnight, and all the ceiling you have for the poor and the suffering and the sick and the halt and the maimed and the blind is about seven million dollars, while we quarrel about whether we shall pay them $5 out of $30, or four or five dollars out of $25. What a miserable sum for such a purpose! No wonder so much suffering exists in the homes of this country ! I remember that the sister of Sir William Mulock, Mrs. Boultbee, who had taken a great deal of interest in homes for infants and other charitable institutions once came and told me, as the mayor of the city, "If you do not give us a larger grant for the infants' home we are going to put the babies on the front steps of the city 
hall." They did not need to do that, because the city of Toronto provided for them generously.
I greatly regret that these social problems have been made a political football ever since I have been in the house. Let us show some Christian charity among ourselves. Never mind who is entitled to the credit so long as the work is done. The poor are suffering, and I am almost ashamed as I travel over the country and visit the homes of the poor, for whom hardly a dollar is spent, while we provide $140 million to erect castles in the air and ceilings on anything or everything. Charity begins at home. Let us find first a few dollars for old age pensions and pensions for the blind. In letters I receive from the troops in Italy and other places the writers want to know if its true that their parents have been laid off work owing to the age limit, or that they are taxed heavily on what little they have, and they wonder what is going to happen to them in trying to exist on the dollar or dollar and a half a day which is about all they get.

I shall not digress
into the history of the old age pension movement, nor shall I enter into argument with those who took part in that battle nearly twenty years ago ; except to say this, that the people of Canada to-day-that goes not only for the old people but for the younger as well -are not half as much interested in who is to receive credit for what was done twenty years ago as in who is to provide them with pensions that will meet the needs of the present day. That, I think, is the vital question we should discuss here to-night.

I am confident that every old person and every pensioner in this country and thousands of younger sons and daughters of these pensioners would be grateful to the minister for the crumbs which have fallen from the treasury bench's table to them These improvements help, and the people of Canada, the old people in particular, will be grateful for the change which has been made in the residential requirements. But there is still much to be done, and I think the most hopeful part of the minister's speech was the promise that he held out that there was to be something better in the near future. While a person now receives a pension at seventy if he has lived sixteen of the last twenty years in Canada, that still leaves many people with unsolved problems. There is a vast number

1Yar Appropriation-Finance
of people in this country, aged and indigent, who reach seventy years of age and yet will not qualify for a pension even under these more generous terms, and I think we have to face the question of just what we are to do with indigent old people. We are not going to give them a pension and many of them will become a burden upon the municipality or the public, and while I am not going to say where that line should be drawn, nevertheless, sooner or later-I hope sooner rather than later-we shall have to accept the responsibility of publicly providing for the old and indigent. And I think we shall have to do it before they reach seventy years of age. As already pointed out, the time is not far distant when we shall be wise enough to know that it will pay us as a people to provide the aged at sixty-five with an adequate income, that it will be advantageous to us to do that, just as it is advantageous now for us to give gifts to the mother country m time of need. We shall find that the money will come back to us, that our entire economy will profit by the money we expend in providing these old people, not at seventy but at a lower age, with an adequate income.
There are two or three regrets I have to express. I wish the minister would correct me if I am wrong, but do I understand that where an old age pensioner receives, on behalf of a son in the armed forces, dependent's allowance, coupled with assigned pay, both the dependent's allowance and the assigned pay are counted as part of the income in arriving at the pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; they are both counted.

That is one of the things I regret. I wish that the minister, when he was amending the act, had taken that into consideration. That assigned pay is the soldier's money, and if he chooses to send it to his father or his aged mother, the government has no right whatever to save on its pensions by adding that to the pensioner's income. I do not think the minister himself : I do not think any cabinet minister; I do not think any member in this house would stand on a public platform anywhere in this country and defend that principle. I am confident that if that question were placed before this house at any time, not even cabinet ministers would support it. I would urge the minister to take that into consideration and, in arriving at the maximum pension, leave the question of assigned pay out of the picture entirely.
There is another matter I regret. The hon member for Winnipeg North Centre called attention to a clause in the act which seemed to provide that the home in which a pensioner lived should not be considered in arriving at
the amount of his income. I have argued this with the officials many times, and I can find nothing in the act itself which justifies the board in taking as part of his income five per cent of the assessed value of the little home in which the pensioner lives. I can find it in the regulations and it appears to me to be a clear case of regulations, formulated by some board, overriding an act passed by parliament. I am confident that the people of this country, I do not care where you go, are opposed to that practice. They are opposed to having five per cent of the assessed value of the home in which the pensioner lives counted as part of his income against his pension.
On these two points I wish the minister would do something to get rid of this injustice. They are unfair and I do not think they can be justified on any grounds. There are other points in the act upon which I will not touch to-night, but in regard to these matters I appeal to the minister.
There is another point I would bring to the minister's attention. A great many instances have been brought to my notice where old people find it impossible to obtain proof of age. I have been told again and again by the officials that proof of age must be documentary evidence of some kind. I will say this for the officials. I have found them most cooperative and ready to accept almost every form of document which would establish, by way of documentary evidence, the date of birth. But a number of cases have been brought to my attention where the officials recognize that people are entitled to pensions but there is no possibility of getting any document sufficiently old to establish their date of birth. The hon. member for Davenport was good enough to refer to many of the old people born in Newfoundland. I have come across many such cases. No vital statistics were kept there until recently. If I had to establish the date of my birth, by a birth certificate, I could not do so. At the time I was born in Newfoundland no vital statistics were kept. There is no record there. I was fortunate enough to have secured an affidavit from my parents when I came to Canada and I have had to use that as documentary evidence when I required proof of age. There are many people from Newfoundland in Canada who just cannot get documentary proof of age. I have tried, in some instances, to get the old school registers, but they cannot be found. We have tried to get evidence from the churches in which persons' baptisms were recorded, but in many instances the churches are burned; the records have been destroyed. I have a number of deserving cases that just simply cannot get proof of

War Appropriation-Finance

age. I think there should be some latitude left to the board or to some officials whereby affidavits or adequate proof of age could be accepted without insisting on documentary evidence as required at the present time. I make these three suggestions to the minister for his consideration.

I should like first of
all to endorse the remarks and arguments
which were so ably set forth this afternoon by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver South. Without repeating any of the arguments that have been made to-day there are one or two points that bother me to some extent. One of them has just been referred to. It is the case of the old age pensioner with a son serving in the armed services. I think it is most unfair, where it can be proven that the son had been contributing to the assistance particularly of a widowed mother.
I think I have discussed this matter of old age pension in every session since I have been here. In 1940 I set forth the idea that those pensioners should receive at least S30 a month or a dollar a day. The cost of living has risen considerably since that time. I think the index is a hundred and nineteen point something now and food is much higher. The cost of food is up thirty per cent in the index. As has been pointed out, many of those old people have been pioneers in this country. At times they thought they had enough laid up for the eventide of their lives. In many instances, through no fault of their own they have lost it. I think we should do better for those old people who have developed this country. We should make better provision for them in their old age. We might consider raising the amount to at least S30 a month. The age limit might be reduced to sixty-five years in the case of males and to sixty years in the case of females.
To return to the matter of the widowed mother with a son serving in the armed services. I do not have to remind this committee that many of those sons are dying for parliament and our way of living to-day. I do not think we are keeping faith with the mothers of those sons who have sacrificed their lives for our way of life. Surely the first move with respect to social security in this country should be by way of a proper provision for those old people who in the eventide of their life are now in difficult circumstances. That should be our first thought in so far as social security in this land of ours is concerned. We all recognize that we have what could easily be, if it is not now, one of the most prosperous lands in the world. We have many untold and undeveloped

natural resources and a sparsely settled country. Surely with all our available resources we can afford to do better for those old people and I think we should rightly do so.
I feel very much concerned about this matter, particularly with respect to those in the armed services. I sincerely trust that the minister will bring down legislation immediately whereby the assigned pay and the old age pension will not be taken into account where dependents' allowance is required.
Before taking my seat I wish to compliment the minister upon the statement he made in this house last month. I think the matter of increasing the income which the pensioner is allowed to earn from $65 to $125 is a step in the right direction, but I do not think it goes far enough. It should be still further increased. I trust that these suggestions, and especially the one about the widowed mother with sons in the armed services, will be dealt with more leniently. It is dealt with now in an altogether too carping a manner.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I wish to say a couple of words on this matter. We have witnessed what I might call the Messiah versus the Messiah versus the Messiah this evening where so many different people have taken credit for the original establishment of old age pensions in this country. I think from a political sense the best exposition that I have heard to-day was from the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I have a definite recollection of following him in the House of Commons in connection with this -Vitally important social problem. In saying that I do not want to take anything away from my good old friend the late James Woodsworth, with whom I sat in this House of Commons, and Abe Heaps. It might be truthfully said that the fact that the Liberal party in 1919 had this as part of its platform gives some indication of the movement in that direction over a good many years. But what has not been said here this evening and what should be said is the contribution made by the trade unions in this country in connection with the establishment of the old age pension.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We are glad to join with you in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
It can be truthfully said that the trade unions as an economic organization-not as a political organization, you understand, because politicians from the very nature of things are very careful sometimes about what they champion-first sponsored in a big way the advocacy of old age pensions in the Dominion of Canada. Because of the observations that have been made here this afternoon and evening I believe it is only fair

War Appropriation-Finance
for me to make that statement. I endeavoured to get from the library here the records of . the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada back to 1894 or somewhere around there, but I was not able to get them. I was able to get only back to 1914. I shall read a resolution advocating old age pensions in this dominion at a time before the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre even lived here. Let us go the correct way about this. Might I also say this, that I played some part in the establishment of old age pensions in this country, if I may be forgiven for saying it in a personal way, because I signed the agreement that brought it into existence in the province of Ontario. Strange to say, one of the signers of the agreement was the Hon. Peter Heenan, who was Minister of Labour of the Dominion of Canada at the time; the other signer was the Hon. Howard Ferguson, who was leader of the Conservative party in Ontario; and I went in and witnessed their signatures. Therefore it might be truthfully said that all the forward-looking citizens of this country who believe in social progress have played their part in the establishment of this very necessary social reform. Let us be fair and honest about it.
I have a vivid recollection of the campaign in which I took some part, the election of 1926, I think it was, referred to by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi. I think it was at that time that the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada set in motion another agitation, an educational agitation, for four fundamental things that were necessary. I remember two of them. One was the abolition of section 98 of the criminal code, and the other one was the establishment, after a veto by the senate, of old age pensions. If I remember rightly, I think the third one was the abolition or reform of the senate. Arising out of that educational campaign we got the establishment of old age pensions.
Might I say that if I had my life to live over again-I advocated non-contributory old age pensions-I think I would advocate contributory old [DOT] age pensions. I believe that pensions should be paid-I speak now as an individual-to the people of this country by right. The only way you can get anything by right is by making some contribution to it. That principle is followed in Great Britain. It has been followed in Sweden and New Zealand, and in any country where they have what might be called a successful old age pension system, it does embody a contributory system.
We hear people talk about non-contributory unemployment insurance and non-contributory this and non-contributory something else. Whether you like it or not, anything and

everything that is paid by the state is a charge on the living standards of the people of this dominion or any other nation. History has proven that pride is the backbone of a nation. Let us consider, for example, the nation from which the hon. member for New Westminster comes. There you have thrift and pride, a combination which has made the Scotch people what they are.	[DOT]
In the very nature of things we must take care of these old people, and I take second place to no man in the House of Commons in my understanding of the obligation owed1 to them by the state. But I hope I shall live to see the day when we shall establish a system of old age pensions which will provide pensions by right to every person-to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and to myself, for that matter, and if necessary to the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway company. I do not think there should be any discrimination whatsoever.	.
Some people are thrifty. It is something like walking down a country lane and seeing different kinds of land. We see the good farmer, the fair farmer, the indifferent or average farmer. Thrift should not stand as a barrier in setting out the obligation of the state toward the old people. It would be my hope that as the days go by we might establish in Canada a system of old age pensions, based upon a contributory principle, the same as unemployment insurance.
I have always felt that there have been three great fears in the lives of working men and women: the fear of destitution in old age, the fear of destitution through sickness, and the fear of destitution through unemployment. I have always felt it is only a question of organization in a big way-in a big way, you understand, rather than by telling people they can have something for nothing-that these fears can be met. There should be organization in a big way, and on a contributory basis, so that a nation could-not in a full measure, perhaps, but at least in a reasonable degree- eliminate those three fears from the lives of its working men and women, its farmers and others engaged in the commercial life of the country.
I have given what I have always considered to be my philosophy of life. It is as old as history itself. And remember this, that any state which started out to kid the people that it was giving something away for nothing, has ended up in the ashcan. It may be that we now have a new formula; I do not know. I sincerely hope, with all my being, that we have. But human nature being what it is, and in the light of history, there is reason for

doubt. One could read the history of Carthage, Rome, Greece, the history of other civilizations and nations-
And Russia.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I could say that, too, but not at the present time. They flourished and decayed. That is written indelibly in the history of those nations. The strength and power of the British people is their pride and thrift. That has made them what they are. I hope that some day I shall live to see worked out an organization operating on a contributory basis which will attack these three great fears of our men, women and children.

Mr. Chairman, various phases of the Old Age Pensions Act have been discussed this afternoon and this evening. However, I should like to touch upon just one phase of it, namely that relating to the blind. In doing so, I should first of all like to refer to that able and energetic blind administrator, Colonel Baker, director of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. That is an institution which has done much more than is realized by the general public. It is to Colonel Baker that this country owes a debt for having made it possible for so many blind persons to maintain themselves.
Then, in the Department of Pensions and National Health is Doctor Burke, who has made a special study of the case for the blind. He has gone into the matter thoroughly, and looks forward to the day when there may be a further step which will improve the condition of the blind, and also relieve them by a system of treatments which should be put into effect in every province. Had such been done in late years, it is altogether probable that many who are now receiving pensions at the reduced age oi forty, many who are to-day shut out from the world, would be relieved of that disability.
It is known that in 1942 there were 12,350 blind persons in Canada. Of that number sonle 6,350 are now pensioned, not only by reason of the age limit of seventy, but by reason of the reduced age of forty. There are also about 2,300 who are not blind, according to the interpretation of that status, as it is defined in the act, but who are suffering, and who would never have reached that state of disability had there been proper treatment. In many instances their condition is the result of disease, or malnutrition, or of accidents.
In this day and age when we look forward to travelling along a trail of sunshine and security the first essential is health. When we do not have the best of health and the best of treatment we may look forward to further cases of blindness, calling for pensions. It is strange to note how the cases are apporfMr. Mitchell.]
tioned among the provinces. Although Ontario has a population which is 400,000 greater than that of Quebec, yet we find that Quebec has about 2,100 oases of blindness, and that about 900 are deserving and desirous of treatment. There are about 2,100 cases in the dominion who are awaiting the eligible age of forty years before they can be pensioned.
The point I would emphasize to-night is the necessity for treatment of the blind. Then, too, I hope the minister may see his way clear in the near future to bring in a measure which will put under one act legislation affecting the blind. I would suggest, too, that the age limit for the blind should be brought down to twenty-one years. Surely the life of a young man is just as valuable at the age of twenty-one years. He has more to look forward to at that age than the man who is blind at the age of forty years. The main purpose of all this social legislation is to create self-maintenance, self-support and independence. We are indebted to Colonel Baker for having made it possible for so many blind persons to be able to maintain themselves. I urge upon the government the providing of treatment in order to prevent so many people from being shut out from the world as the blind are. I ask the minister to give thought to this suggestion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not been one who has been favourable to rising by way of repetition of other people's arguments, and I have no desire to do so to-night. I join with many of those who have spoken. There was an air of unanimity in the committee, to ask and demand that the older people of Canada shall have a square deal. I want to say to the government and to those in the committee that it seems to be easy for promises to be made and for bidding sometimes to take place with respect to the older people in our land. I may say that what the older people are interested in are not promises, what the older people are interested in is action which will bring them the conditions to which they are entitled under the present situation.
I want to say to the committee, and I state it very seriously, that I believe in the days to come the course outlined by the hon. member for Vancouver South must be followed by the Canadian people in a way in which it has never been followed before. That is, human values must definitely replace material values in a way that we in this nation have never known before. That is one of the things which the new era, the new world, the new order, will call for, will demand and must get if it is to be successful.

War Appropriation-Finance
I would say this one thing with respect to old age pensions. This party does not take a back seat to any party in the House of Commons in its desire-perhaps this is more important-and in the years to come in its capacity to do something for those of our older people in Canada. As I listened to the hon. member for Kootenay West I could not help thinking of the excellent address that was made last night to the empire parliamentary association group in Ottawa by Mr. George Tomlinson, undersecretary to the minister of labour of Great Britain. He indicated the work that was being done there in rehabilitation in connection with those who have lost their sight. He pointed out that in certain industries in Britain those who are unable to see have mastered certain jobs which could not be mastered in the same way by those who have their sight. This was of vast interest to those who listened to him. I think we were all much cheered with the thought that there were jobs and trades being created for our people who are thus afflicted.
I rose to-night more particularly to say to the minister that there is one thing that perhaps ought to be stressed at this time. I have had cases, and I imagine hon. members have had cases, where old age pensions have been reduced, sometimes taken away entirely, because assigned pay or dependents' allowance had been received by a mother of a boy who is overseas. I want to make this very earnest plea to the minister and I think it is one that he will at once see should be given consideration. Where there is assigned pay or where there is a dependents' allowance I do not think this country can afford-I put it as seriously as that-to ignore the situation where those people are being so treated with respect to the reduction in old age pension, or in some instances are experiencing its loss altogether. It certainly is not fair and it certainly is not understood by those who are thus involved. From the cases I have come across I have reached the conclusion that we must do away with the regulation which calls for that.
Curiously enough, just a short time ago I received definite information and evidence of one particular case concerning two old people. The old gentleman was receiving an old age pension. His wife is living and his son is overseas. Assigned pay and dependents' allowance were paid into that home. First of all, his pension was taken away and then on May 12 last it was restored to the extent that instead of receiving $25 he now receives $12.83. I do not want to be unduly critical of the minister, and I do not rise in any sense of narrow criticism, but I think this
country and this government will at once recognize that that is not the way to increase confidence in those fine old citizens of our country whose sons are overseas fighting for the security which we enjoy.
I for one do not think-and I believe I speak on behalf of the committee generally- that we can afford to allow that state of affairs to continue in this dominion. It may ' seem a small item to some people; it may seem a very insignificant thing, but when one realizes that this is the one and only source' of revenue and income that some people have, it becomes a matter of major importance to them. I want to make the plea to the minister sincerely to-night that something be done with respect to the situation which I have just described. I realize that there has been some change made, but evidently the situation still needs attention of the character I have indicated. .

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate that the minister wants to get his estimates through, but I have a few observations I should like to make. I have sat here for some time and had someone else expressed what I had in mind, I would not be on my feet at this moment. I wish to request the minister to pay serious attention to the remarks to-night of the hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard. Increasing the old- age pension and the pension to the blind would not be a waste of money. There is a great consuming market in these people. There are 188,488 people receiving pensions, and there are a great number who do not receive them, particularly blind persons, because the blind pension is not paid until forty years of age.
I think that is a crime. If you doubled the old age pension all the money would be spent within Canada. It would stimulate the markets across Canada and help in building up this country. I am not going to go into that in any detail because it is elementary social economics.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But a post-war argument.

That is so, and it is post-war that I am thinking,of. I realize that after the close of this session we may have an election, and we do not know who will be in power next. In listening to the debate in the house to-night, I have wondered who is the government of this country. Conservative members, whose party has been in power many times in the last seventy-six years, claim that on every occasion that their party has been in power the old age pension has been very close to their hearts The same is said by the Liberal members, who claim credit for establishing what? We have not established
War Appropriation-Finance

old age pensions in Canada yet. What makes me wonder who is running this country and who has been running it in the past is that the members of the House of Commons, we who are sent here to legislate for this country and are desirous of seeing old age pensions established, and the aged and the blind get everything that is coming to them, have not brought this thing to pass. What has stopped them from doing it? All that is required is to bring down the necessary legislation and it would go through the house unanimously.
I am sorry for the Minister of Finance, for whose honesty I have a great deal of respect.
I am led to believe, after listening to the discussion here to-night, that whoever sits behind the scenes and runs the treasury board is running this country. Otherwise we would give effect to the things we talk about wanting. That is what strikes me as I sit here. If I belonged to a party in this house that had -been in power in this country in the last twenty or thirty or forty years I certainly would not want to rise in this house and say that I still owed allegiance to that party and supported its principles if it had neglected the opportunity of passing the legislation when it was within its power to do so. That would be an admission that, while in office, it had not taken advantage of its privilege to enact the necessary legislation which it said it wanted.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Labour mention the struggle which had been made by the labour unions across Canada during the past forty years to get the old age pension enacted. Yes, they have struggled, and struggled hard. They have passed resolutions at their conventions, provincial, national and local, but they had no power to legislate. I can remember back to the year 1910, when I sat in a very small provincial organization in Nova Scotia which passed resolutions favouring old age pensions. They have been trying all along to get the government to do something about it.
What struck me to-night in the analysis given by the Minister of Labour of contributory and non-contributory old age pension schemes is this, that there is no such thing as a non-contributory old age pension scheme. You do not get anything without contributing toward it. I have said that for the last twenty years, when many people were discussing a non-contributory system. Our aged people have made their contribution. They have gone into industry or worked on the farms or in business; they have raised their families and given their children of three generations to war; they have helped to build this nation. Now they are at the end of the trail when they are no longer productive, and they are
[Mr. Gillis.l	.
relegated to the scrap-heap. I have in mind the heavy industries of this country. I should like some members of the house to go into the coal mines of Nova Scotia at five o'clock in the morning and watch the old men, seventy years of age and older, with a can on their backs, hobbling along with a cane perhaps, crippled, but obliged to work because they have no other means of livelihood. They have given everything they had to that industry and there is nothing for them at the end of the trail. They have made their contribution already. That is why I say there is no such thing as a non-contributory system.
The minister stated that New Zealand and other countries had a contributory scheme. That is true. But he failed to point out the different methods used in those countries to finance their social security scheme. New Zealand has an over-all social security plan, covering old age pensions, medicine and all the rest of it-all these schemes that we are considering separately. Theirs is the only way to do it. New Zealand has a five per cent tax against all income in New Zealand, and the proceeds from that tax go into their over-all social security fund, which provides for old age pensions as well as other things. Everyone contributes to it. If your income is small, you make your contribution; if your income is larger, you make a greater contribution. It is a direct tax on the pay envelope of the individual. Everyone pays into that social security fund on the basis of his ability to pay. That is the difference in New Zealand.

I am not going to argue with the hon. member. The tax I mentioned is the tax that has been in effect in New Zealand up until six months ago. It may have been changed recently. That is the only way in . which to deal with the matter. If you are going to finance separately all the social security plans that are being discussed in Canada now, $12 a year for medical services, so much for unemployment insurance, and so on, and load all those charges back against the pay envelope of the individual, or apply it as a tax by municipalities upon property, it will never work. No one can make it work. The only way in which to work it is the way they have in New Zealand.
I agree with the minister that we shall have to understand what is contributory and what is not. But I maintain that there is no such thing as a non-contributory scheme. We have to pay for it out of the wealth that is produced in this country. Personally I would not want to take any credit for the old age pension scheme that we have in effect to-day. We have established the principle; that is about all; and as someone pointed out here to-night, it really is a paupers' allowance, because the thing which any applicant for the old age pension to-day has to prove is that he is a pauper, that he does not own anything. Take, for example, the sad experience of certain families of veterans of the last war. The men carry an insurance policy of a thousand dollars. They pass away. They are no sooner dead than someone from the old age pension board and the other bodies which handed them out pittances comes in to inquire if there was any insurance. "Yes; there was a thousand dollars insurance." "All right, you cannot get anything from any source, be it a mother's allowance or anything else, until you have spent that thousand dollars insurance and have rendered an itemized account of it to the different boards from which you expect help, so as to make sure that it is all gone and that you have spent it solely for the necessities of life." These things are nothing to brag about.
I would be ashamed if I had to admit that 1 had ever sat on a committee and put my name to that kind of legislation.

As regards that thousand dollars, Mr. Chairman, is it not a fact that they figure out how much of an annuity could be purchased at the age of the pensioner, and then calculate, not the principal itself but the amount which would be produced if it were used to buy a government annuity?	[DOT]
No.
I think it is.
That thousand dollars has to be used up. In the old age pension scheme they watch it a little closer. I am talking now about the application of the old age pension in Nova Scotia.
We have a better scheme in Alberta.
Hear, hear.
I am not going to get into a political argument about Alberta. I know you have. I might go farther and say that it is not a Liberal or a Tory government in Alberta.
Nor a C.C.F. government.

That is true. I know old people who dragged out their lives in the coal mines, retired at seventy, applied for the old age pension, and when a check-up was made, it was found that they had a few hundred dollars in the bank to pay the cost of burying
them.

I have always wondered why the province from which the hon. member for Cape Breton South comes has always paid the lowest old age pension of the provinces. As you know, it started at S20; some pay $30; but in Nova Scotia I believe the average is around $11; and I never could understand how a person could live on that, and why the province has not increased it.

You cannot live on it, and the only answer I can give is that up to 1925 we had about forty-six years of Liberal government in Nova Scotia. There was a break
then,	when the Tories went in, but the Liberals went back in again.
