In checking the thing since the rates were changed and the increase was granted, I have been told that there has been a much stricter administration, and that people actually lost money. That is all they succeeded in doing there with the increase.
There are two things of which I want specifically to complain in the administration of the act. A soldier of the last war who served in a theatre of war and is in receipt of war veteran's allowance is granted that pension because of being incapacitated through service in an actual theatre of war. The pension is granted by the federal government, and is the veteran's pension by right. Two cases have been brought to my attention where a wife, having reached the age of seventy, made application for old age pension, and S12 a month was granted and payment made for about two years. Then someone advised the authorities that the husband was in receipt of a "burnt-out" pension of S30 or S40 a month, whereupon the old age pension of the wife was immediately . discontinued, and the war veteran's allowance to the husband was assessed so much a month to pay back what had been paid to the wife by way of old age pension. I think that is a practice which should be discontinued.
The same principle applies in the matter of compensation. A man injured in industry is in receipt of compensation, for which benefit he has paid. Some people are of the opinion that it is a benevolent set-up, that in the case of accident the industrialist pays you because of the injury. One of the first charges against the wage rates of workers in industry is compensation. It is one of the major elements in computing cost of production.
But the worker pays only a percentage.
He pays a big percentage.
No; small.
The fact of the matter is-if you want to argue the matter-that he pays it all. There is nobody who produces except the worker.
Not in Alberta.

Just a minute. In a steel plant, in a coal mine, in a factory or a mill, the only person who produces wealth in the industry is the person who actually works. Nobody else produces it; and when you sit in and make an assessment for compensation purposes, if you pay only twenty-five or thirty per cent it is taken out of the actual cost of the operation, and he is the man who pays the shot 100 per cent. But in the event of an injury, and the man receives a small pension

to compensate for the partial or permanent disability, there is an arrangement that, in the event of old age pension being paid, it is deductible from what the man receives in compensation pension. We are only kidding people when we tell them that we have estab-lishesd an old age pension system for the aged and infirm when we ramify it through every other piece of legislation we have in operation. Either it is an old age pension or it is not. I believe that the first charge on the wealth of this and any country is for the care of the aged. I believe they should receive that pension when they are sixty years of age. There is no use in giving it to either a man or a woman who is older than that. What can they do with it? They cannot enjoy life; they cannot get around. They cannot do anything with it. When anyone has struggled from the time he or she is twenty years of age until the age of sixty and made a contribution in this country, the statesmen who are running the country should recognize it _ as an obligation to see that the few remaining years of his or her life are spent in at least a fair degree of comfort, with enough to eat, enough to wear, some little recreation and the opportunity to breathe the fresh air. That is not asking too much; it is a right which should be recognized; no strings should be attached to it, and there should be no quibbling about it.
I have heard no little talk about the building of morale of the men in the armed services. In listening this evening to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and some other speakers, it struck me that if the programme of policy of the Liberal party as laid down in 1919 had been implemented even to the extent of fifty per cent, there would not be these groups in this chamber to-night. The groups represented here are the logical protest against promises made and never fulfilled. Fifty per cent of the programme mapped out in 1919, had it been put into effect, would, I am reasonably sure, have offset the third party movements in this country. But we have passed the time when we can keep on merely promising.
We have to start doing something, and on this point alone I think that at this session of the house something should be done about old age pensions. I think for the moment of the hundreds of boys in fox-holes in Italy and of the thousands who are waiting to-night in England to go on board a barge to cross the channel. They know what they are going into and they stop and look back at Canada and wonder what is happening here. You know that many of the homes these boys come from have as their only income an assignment of pay. In some cases they have

War Appropriation-Finance
an allowance by virtue of that assignment of pay. If something happens to that boy during the process of crossing the channel and going into the land of the enemy, that assignment of pay will stop; that allowance to the family will be discontinued. The result is that that family has a good chance of going back on relief. That is not a good state of mind for that boy to be in when he goes to invade the European continent.
In my opinion, one of the greatest morale builders that could be provided for the services at this time, and for our old people as well, would be a declaration on the part of the federal government that we in this country have enacted an old age pension law that will guarantee to the aged, at the age of sixty or sixty-five, an income of around $40 a month. It is the right of the old people; it is something they are entitled to; and if they have built a little home for themselves, if they have accumulated something in the course of their lifetime, there is no reason why they should be penalized in consequence and have to will that home to the provincial government in order to establish their right to pension. If something were done along the line I have suggested it would establish the morale of the men. I know it would be a relief to me if I were in England to-night, about to cross the channel, to know that we in Canada had taken at least one step in the direction of guaranteeing a measure of security to the people I had left behind.
And remember that the boys who are going to cross the channel come largely from such families. The one thing that I have feared, the one thing that ninety per cent of our people have feared all their lives, is old age. There is no security. You are living ninety per cent of your life preparing yourself to get sufficient to bury you after you leave this earth. That is all. The fear of insecurity is the spectre that has haunted the great majority of the people of this country. I do not know what the minister will do about it. But I am reasonably sure that if he has his way he will do something about it. I fear, however, that someone else is superior to him behind the scenes, and that is why something has not been done long ago.
Sitting here, listening to the discussion, I wonder where the supremacy of parliament is. This is not a war measure that must be passed by order in council. It is something that comes within the purview of the House of Commons, and we are all agreed upon it. Why, therefore, do we not do something about it? What are we waiting for? I could stand here and talk for hours on this subject, but I will not do so. The hon. member for
Kootenay West spoke also about the blind pensioners, and they are in a worse position, if anything. There are hundreds of blind people in the country who are receiving no pension. Up to forty years of age you may be stone blind and yet not receive anything. After you pass forty years of age they will make some provision for you. There is a possibility that if there were proper pensions and grants and provisions made to augment the schools throughout the country, hundreds of young people who are in that condition could be made productive, and helped to lead useful lives.
I could tell the committee a story of the administration of blind pensions, but I will not do so now. It is too long. Certainly it leaves much to be desired. The people who are obliged to live either on a war pension or on a compensation pension and who are unfortunate enough to have a blind boy or girl in the house are penalized if they send that boy or girl to school. If the child is in the home the blind pension is paid, or the compensation pension is paid, on behalf of that child; but if that child is sent to Halifax, to a blind school, from any part of Nova Scotia, then immediately he leaves home and becomes an extra responsibility the pension is cut off, because he is no longer living at home. That is crazy, because the fact that the child has gone to a school adds to the obligations on the mother, in the case I have in mind, instead of relieving her. The compensation pension was cut off because he left his home and went into a school in Halifax.
It is little odds and ends such as this that irritate the people. In connection with this matter of compensation, war veterans' allowance, an agreement or understanding arrived at between the federal government and the provincial authorities is, I think, something which, if the Minister of Finance has any authority or power over, he should put his foot on. If a man is burnt out and unemployable in consequence of service in- an actual theatre of war, what he receives is his by right, and if his wife is blind she should be entitled to blind pension, without any interference with what has already been granted the soldier by statute. The same applies to compensation. The compensation paid should not militate against the wife in the event of her reaching the age prescribed by the act in making her eligible for old age pension. This is something I feel strongly about, because it is one thing which for many years I have thought over. I have sat down and drafted bills, dozens of them. I have had pilgrimages to the provincial governments. We have tried to make it contributory; we have tried to

make applicable to our own industry, we have tried in every way to get around it, but we have met with a rebuff every time. If we established it for one industry we were told we would have to make it contributory for some others; the rural people would make a fuss if it were not applicable to them, and we have not the same access to them by way of contributions, and so forth. For years and years we have been going around in a circle trying to do something about, the matter. It is a federal responsibility. Everyone is agreed on that, but the surprising thing is that we do not do something about it.
